text:
Senate Democrats are working to short-circuit a bill aimed at protecting consumers from the costs of data centers.

The Ratepayer Protection Act passed the House 417-3 in the 435-member House.

However, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer opposes the bill, which he called “a fraud,” according to The Hill.

“Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, but all the Republicans offer is a toothless messaging bill,” he said Tuesday.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R- SD) on the Ratepayer Protection Act vote tomorrow: “It ought to be a no brainer here on the floor of the Senate.”The bill, which aims to lower energy costs from data centers, passed 417-3 in the House of Representatives on Sept. 16. https://t.co/exxKLBrLJK— Summer Hu (@Summer_Huu) September 29, 2026

The bill requires 60 votes to pass a procedural hurdle. Although Republicans have a majority in the Senate, it would take Democratic votes to move the bill forward.

Democratic Sen. Peter Welch of Vermont, who had been the lone Democrat supporting the bill, said he has changed his mind.

“We want to get a real Ratepayer Protection Act,” he said. “I’m for ratepayer protections. This bill doesn’t do anything.”

The bill introduced by Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio requires states to consider imposing a regulatory structure in which data centers pay for energy costs and any power grid updates.

The bill does not require states to impose costs on data centers, leading Democratic Sen. Gary Peters to snark, “I wish it actually had some teeth.”

.@SenJonHusted‘s Ratepayer Protection Act passed the House 417-3. That’s overwhelming support. Yet, Democrats in the Senate stand in the way of relief.Tomorrow, Democrats can join Republicans and help lower costs or they can explain why they’re standing in the way of relief. https://t.co/zfbFtCJDsA— Sen. John Barrasso (@SenJohnBarrasso) September 29, 2026

After House passage of the bill, Republicans noted that it effectively insulated consumers from the costs of data centers.

“When done responsibly, data center development leads to longer term investments and broader infrastructure improvements in the communities where they’re built,” Republican Rep. Brett Guthrie of Kentucky said. “The Ratepayer Protection Act helps to safeguard these benefits by ensuring that the companies who are building data centers — and not American families and small businesses — are paying for the electricity they use.”

“U.S. leadership in the race to AI dominance is critical to our economic prosperity and national security, so we need to keep building the needed infrastructure with appropriate accountability measures,” he added. “I’m grateful to Congressman Evans for his tireless work — on a bipartisan basis — to protect ratepayers while ensuring that America continues to lead the world in innovation,” he said.

Sen. @JonHusted (R-OH) on Ratepayer Protection Act: “This is the only bill that has a chance to pass before the election…206 Democrats voted for it…if we want to prove to the American people before the midterm elections, whose side we’re on, this is the only chance.” https://t.co/RWu4aqwsAV— CSPAN (@cspan) September 29, 2026

Republican Rep. Gabe Evans of Colorado said, “Hardworking families should not have to subsidize the energy demands of data centers. America needs the infrastructure to lead the world in AI and outcompete Communist China, but we cannot have that growth at the expense of hardworking families, farmers, seniors, and small businesses.

“My bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act ensures large data centers pay for the infrastructure they require while giving states the flexibility to determine what works best for their communities. I’m incredibly proud to lead the charge on this pivotal issue, ensure our ratepayers are protected, and keep American innovation moving forward,” he said.

This article appeared originally on The Western Journal.

text:
This is how the Ayatollahs fooled the Iranian people and the Islamic world.

Shia Iran has nothing to do with the Sunni problem of Palestine or Israel, located thousands of miles away, sharing no borders, no clash of national interests, and no history of dispute.

Making the Israel-Palestinian issue central to its foreign policy is sheer opportunism and geopolitics, an attempt to justify Iran’s hidden motive to dominate the Sunni Middle East. The only military power that stops Iran is Israel; hence destroying Israel became a national goal. The Palestinian cause was adopted not to give Palestinians a state, but to justify hostile policies toward Israel and clear the way for regional ambitions.

Religious sentiments are provoked in the name of Al-Aqsa Mosque. Unlike what Muslim conquerors often did to non-Islamic places of worship, Israel did not destroy Al-Aqsa. It allows Muslims to pray there and will continue to do so. So what is the problem?

These are made-up issues to fool foolish Muslims into laying down their cheap lives in the name of martyrdom so leaders can assume power and privileges for themselves, not for you. These religious leaders want you to die for stupid, invented stories.

As for the Palestinian problem, in 1948 a two-state solution was offered. They refused, attacked, and lost.

Gaza was occupied by Egypt and the West Bank by Jordan, then annexed; the West Bank’s ethnic Jordanian Arab population was given full Jordanian citizenship. For the next 20 years the Gaza and West Bank populations lived under Egyptian and Jordanian rule. Some 700,000 refugees were absorbed in neighboring states, as Israel absorbed 850,000 Jewish refugees displaced from neighboring Arab Muslim countries. India and Pakistan absorbed 6 million displaced refugees after partition; Europeans absorbed millions of displaced European refugees.

The problem was solved. But the Arabs did not want to solve the refugee problem. They wanted to destroy Israel. So the 1967 war took place. Egypt, Syria, Lebanon, and Jordan lost. They lost Gaza, the West Bank, and the Golan Heights to Israel. That was the consequence of war.

You wage war, you lose it, you give away territory to the winner to buy peace. The West Bank was no longer Palestinian territory after Jordan’s 1948 annexation as sovereign territory. When Jordan lost in 1967, it ceded its sovereign Jordanian territories in the West Bank to Israel under a peace treaty. Palestine did not exist then; it had ceased to exist after the 1948 war and annexation of the West Bank into Jordan.

Hence the claim that Israel occupies Palestinian land in the West Bank is utterly false and a wrong narrative—that is why it will always fail. Iran, sitting thousands of kilometers away, has no business meddling in this vexed Palestinian affair.

The Palestinian issue is a Sunni problem. Let the Sunni Arab states and Israel sort it out through the Abraham Accords.

But no: Iran wanted to sabotage Saudi Arabia signing the Abraham Accords that would settle the Palestinian issue once and for all and sideline Iran’s regional ambition to dominate the Sunni Middle East. So it unleashed October 7 through its proxies Hamas and Hezbollah. That went out of its hands and brought the Middle East to this state.

Iran fooling innocent, naive, history-blind, ill-informed people with the sugar-coated claim that it has never attacked any neighboring country is utterly false. Iran rarely attacks directly; it does so through proxies like Hamas and Hezbollah, and it attacks the Saudis through the Houthis, whom it arms, finances, trains, and controls.

So whom are you fooling?

text:
Start here.

A war-band can take a peninsula and still not own its own story. Muhammad died in Medina in June 632. Within a generation his men were not reciting one fixed text. According to the Sunni canon itself—Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 and 5102—Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, campaigning in Armenia and Azerbaijan under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan (r. 644–656), heard Syrian and Iraqi soldiers accusing one another over variant readings of the Qur’an and feared schism. Uthman ordered Zayd ibn Thabit and a small committee to produce one official recension from the sheets already gathered under Abu Bakr after the battle of Yamamah (c. 632–633), sent copies to the main garrison cities, and commanded that other written collections be burned. That is not how a father handles truth. That is how a commander handles a riot in camp. The man of the raid had offered fighting men what fighting men already priced—women, spoil, rank, a paradise with the smell of victory on it—and he got his army: Hijrah 622, Badr 624, the taking of Mecca in 630, a community armed enough that, after 632, it walked out of Arabia and broke the near frontiers of Byzantium and Ctesiphon. He did not get control of the wording. The sword can gather a host. It cannot keep ten mouths from rewriting the banner. When the banner starts a fight, the caliph does not repent. He lights a fire under the other pages (Bukhari 4987).

That is the method. Feed the pack. Win the ground. When the story cracks, burn the variants. A hunter plates the hunger. He does not remake it.

Now the other table.

The gospel is still the worst product in the shop. No one designing customers writes it. Someone who wants sons writes it. Soft men swollen with appetite will always walk to the louder stall. That walk is not evidence. It is the x-ray. And it leaves Jesus where He stands: above the stall, the legion, and every cheap replacement—worthy, because He refused to purchase us with our vice. He paid in blood.

God is not recruiting buyers. He is calling children home.

Jesus does not bait Jew or Greek with their favorite dish. He orders both to drop the plate.

The Jew wanted a war-crown: Rome thrown off, Zion armed, a Messiah who wins like Caesar. Jesus answers with timber and nails, under Pontius Pilate, c. 30–33. “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Come back to the Father. Receive a name. “To all who received Him, He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12).

The Gentile wanted the old night: the body as shrine, the feast that never closes, the rot Paul names in the streets around the churches (Romans 1; 1 Corinthians 5–6). Jesus answers with a cut. Stop staring. Tear out the eye (Matthew 5:27–32). One covenant bed. Rule the flesh. Then live as a son, not as a stomach.

He does not toss steak to the wolf. He puts bread in a mouth that only knew raw meat—and then dies and rises so the mouth can say Abba. No harem as wages. Adoption. The Lamb dies for the enemy. The stone rolls.

Muhammad runs the opposite shop. He wanted a host and he bought one with the inventory the host already priced: raids for caravan wealth after 622, plural marriage written into law, captives as a lawful yield of war. That raises banners. It does not raise sons of God. And when the inventory of words would not sit still, Uthman, about 650–653, burned the extras. Army first. Canon by bonfire second.

Look at what grows, without perfume. Where Christ’s gospel actually entered—not the costume of Christ, the command of Christ—even under crooked kings, a strange orchard appeared: the weak life counts, the child is not a clan chip only, the woman is not a share of loot, letters and universities sprout because a soul is addressed by God and must learn to answer. Cathedral schools and the medieval universitas—Bologna (1088), Paris (c. 1150), Oxford (c. 1096)—did not grow from a tent of captives. They grew from a Cross and from “let the little children come to Me” (Mark 10:14).

A creed built to please the raider will not pause and see woman and child as the image of God. It will see them as cargo—flesh, hush, wall. Useful falsehood, sanctified war, the killing of the holdout, poverty called fate: that is not bad weather on the map. That is what you plant when desire wears a scabbard.

If truth were the average male wish, heaven would be unemployed. We already know the wish: more body, more force, more alibi. That wish is the clay of this century—in the old paganism that still rides under a prophet’s name, and in the new ideologies that spit on the church. Both want a homemade god. One names it caliphate. One names it State. Both say the vote of man is the verdict of right. That sentence is not faith. It is apostasy with a flag.

The hunter blesses the pulse. The Father breaks it and names it child. That is why the gospel still will not sell to synagogue or forum. And that is why Jesus still has no rival: He would rather lose the crowd than nurse the fever. He lost the crowd. He kept the empty tomb. He kept the way back to the Father.

Savior syndrome is not compassion. It is thirst for a throne.

When a man refuses Jesus Christ, he does not end up with no god. He ends up with a lesser god: himself. And because one man cannot save the world, he invents the machine that pretends to omnipotence — the State. Not the state that punishes crime and guards the border. The God-State: the one that defines the good, defines the truth, educates the child, acquits sin and condemns conscience.

This is religion without the Cross. It has sinners (everyone else). It has priests (the “awakened”). It has inquisitors (whoever disagrees). It has a paradise (the project). It only lacks repentance. Because the savior of the syndrome never kneels. He administers.

In the mind of those who do not believe in the Son of God, humanity is a broken mass waiting for a redeemer in an office. Without Christ, someone must take the place. That is where political messianism is born: “we will fix man.” Not convert him. Fix him. Shape him. Re-educate him. Censor the error until the error changes its name.

The Bible already had a name for this.

“You will be like God, knowing good and evil.”
— Genesis 3:5

Hell’s first politics was this: usurp the standard. Not merely to sin — to legislate sin. To decide what is good. To decide what is true. To trade light for darkness and still call it justice.

“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil.”
— Isaiah 5:20

The God-State needs that. Without rewriting the dictionary, it cannot reign. It needs family to become oppression, sin to become identity, limits to become hate, the fear of God to become backwardness. It needs a people who ask salvation from a ministry and not from the Lamb.

This is not the property of one party label. Pagan empires, revolutions, personality cults, and “humanitarian” bureaucracies have drunk from the same cup: man in the place of God. But the impulse is the same whenever a global left pretends to be the secular church of the planet — a gospel without forgiveness, a pulpit without Scripture, a paradise without judgment. Humanity as a project. The elite as a priesthood. Dissent as sin against the party of goodness.

They feel like saviors because they cannot bear to be creatures. A creature needs a Lord. A stage savior needs subjects.

Scripture tears off the disguise:

“The heart is deceitful above all things.”
— Jeremiah 17:9

Whoever does not believe that must believe the problem is only “structure,” “the system,” “the people behind us.” Then the remedy is always more power for those who think themselves pure. More State. More guardianship. More official truth. More silence for anyone who still says there is a good that was not put to a vote.

Yes: there is an adversary behind it. Not as a cheap excuse to stop thinking. As a spiritual diagnosis. The devil does not need a man to wear a costume. He needs a man who wants to be light without Christ.

“For Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.”
— 2 Corinthians 11:14

“He was a murderer from the beginning… because there is no truth in him.”
— John 8:44

The pattern is ancient: offer bread, spectacle, and meaning — provided you bow. In the wilderness the offer to Jesus was exactly that: the kingdoms of the world in exchange for one genuflection. Christ refused. Political messianism accepts. It takes the shortcut. It takes the throne now. It tries to save the world without each man’s cross.

That is why the speech sounds pious and the method is hard. They want the orphan, but often against the father. They want the poor, but often against the moral limit that pulls people out of misery. They want the victim, but often against the truth that the victim also sins. The savior of the syndrome needs eternal victims. The only eternal saint can be himself.

The Christian difference is offensive precisely here: the Savior has already come, and He was not a committee. Jesus Christ does not ask for an omniscient State. He asks for a surrendered heart. He does not outsource good and evil to a cabinet. He writes the law on the conscience and will judge kings.

Whoever mocks this does not become an adult. He becomes an orphan with power. And an orphan with power builds an altar in the Palace.

Man does not need a God-State. He needs to be converted. Without that, every generation invents a new messiah, a new truth, a new good — and calls progress the same stroke of Eden: “we decide.”

They do not decide. They are being used. The theater is salvation. The script is usurpation. And the end of every clay god is the same: the clay returns to dust, and the judgment does not ask what the slogan was.

Think like a simple scientist.

You have three facts, like three stones on the table:

The human cup is cracked. History is full of bones.
Even so, we point and say, “That is wrong” — even when it is our own team.
A cracked cup cannot be the ruler that measures the cup.

In science, when the cup cannot be the ruler, you look for a ruler outside the cup. Nobody measures a meter with a bent meter. Nobody says the north is the boat. The boat turns. The north does not.

Now test the rival ideas, the way you test a theory:

“Good is whatever the tribe likes.”
But we accuse our own tribe. Theory killed by the data.

“Good is whatever the king commands.”
But we accuse the king. Theory killed.

“Good is whatever the strong can do.”
But we call the strong a criminal, not a winner. Theory killed.

One explanation is left that holds all three facts together: there is a Reference that is not the team. A Ruler above the human judge. Without that Ruler, “wrong” is only a taste. With it, “wrong” is true. You already talk as if it were true. You are using the tool and denying the workshop.

That Reference is God.
In flesh, it is Jesus Christ: not a club that got a good grade. He is the test in person.

Take Him away. Good becomes again the fist of the strongest.

This is not finding God under a microscope. It is the same step science takes when it picks the theory that explains the data without cheating. The data are the crack, the pile of bones, and your anger at the pile. Together they do not point to man. They point up.

The cup is still cracked.
The Ruler is not.
You inherited the measure.
Do not pretend you invented it in the laboratory of “me.”

And here is the most important part.

When whole societies took that idea into the state — a state without Christianity’s diagnosis — they did not become free adults at last. They removed the church. They removed the Reference of what is good. Then they proved Christ was always right: man is not good by nature, and he cannot stay good for long without the perfect Reference, which is God.

Atheism is older than Marx. A lonely skeptic in a café is not a civilization. What was new was this: communism put unbelief in the palace, in the school, in the secret police, and called it science. It used the most powerful machine on earth — the modern state — to preach that there is no God, no fall, no sin, only systems and enemies of the people. Tear out the root. The new man will grow.

He did not grow.

He starved. He informed. He filled the grave.

The Soviet Union: Cheka, Gulag, engineered hunger. In Ukraine, 1932–1933, the Holodomor — grain taken, borders sealed, villages blacklisted. Millions dead. Stalin’s purges shot the party itself. The Black Book of Communism puts the Soviet dead on the order of twenty million. Count as you will. The order of magnitude does not become small.

Mao’s China: the Great Leap Forward, 1958–1962 — the deadliest famine in the record of man. Then the Cultural Revolution, children taught to smash the “four olds,” including the soul. The same Black Book assigns China on the order of sixty-five million. Other tallies run higher or lower. None of them look like “humanity finally grown up.”

Cambodia, 1975–1979: Year Zero. Pol Pot emptied the cities, murdered the glasses-wearers, the teachers, the believers. About two million — a quarter of a nation — in less than four years. That is not “religion doing India.” That is the Reference ripped out and the jar worshiping itself.

Across the file — USSR, China, Cambodia, North Korea, Ethiopia under the Derg, the list does not stay local — Courtois and his colleagues reached a grim working total near one hundred million. Scholars argue the edges. They do not argue that the mountain is a molehill. Atheism had existed for centuries. Communism gave it tanks, ration cards, and a curriculum.

This is the experiment the critic asked for.

Remove the diagnosis: man is flawed.
Replace it with: man is clay for the Party.
Remove God as the Régua.
Install history as god.
Then watch the strong call murder “progress.”

Christ said no one is good but God. The twentieth century wrote that sentence in mass graves and called it a five-year plan.

You inherited a morality that still flinches at those graves. That flinch is not Marx. Marx gave you the permission structure: if there is no Judge above the state, the state will judge without mercy. You kept the horror. You forgot the Voice that told you why horror is not “necessary.”

No God, no fall, no limit — only power and a future tense.
That is not enlightenment. That is Eden again: “you will be as gods.”
The fruit was not knowledge. The fruit was a body count.

The jar without water does not become a fountain. It becomes a weapon.
The people without a Reference do not become good. They become busy.

So when the critic says he got his morals from secular philosophers after 1789, point him past the salon to the century that tested the thesis with the full weight of the state. The thesis failed in blood. Christ did not fail. He had already named the patient.

Man is not the Régua.
God is.
Take away that Reference and the world does not rise. It counts its dead — and still pretends the Accuser was the problem.

The folded metro line is the whole argument. We keep using a standard we insist we invented, and then feign shock when the cup leaks. The story is simply the set of data that points to the truth!

“The folded metro line is the whole argument.”
Think of a subway map. A straight line would be man choosing his own path — Eden, “I will name good and evil.” The fold is the break in history: Christ. After Him the moral map of the West and the World no longer follows the old pagan track (the arena, the exposed infant, the slave as a tool, the widow on the pyre). The shape of our conscience is already bent toward the gospel. You do not need a long speech. The map itself gives the origin away.

“We keep using a standard we swear we invented.”
Equal dignity, care for the weak, horror at slavery, at the discarded child, at the girl as a prize of war — many people treat this as “obvious,” “human,” “modern.” The point is that it is not obvious. Rome and Greece did not teach it. The rule we use to judge the world is Christian, even when the judge claims to be secular.

“Then we act shocked when the cup leaks.”
The cup is the Christian, the church, the so-called Christian nation. It is cracked: it sins, it oppresses, it contradicts Jesus. The critic points at the leak and thinks Christ is refuted. The answer is: the leak proves the biblical diagnosis (the jar is clay). It does not cancel the water (Christ). The shock still uses Christ’s ruler against people who failed Christ.

“History is not opinion. It is the dataset agreeing with you.”
This is not only a sermon. It is a repeating pattern. Consciences shifted after the gospel. Hospitals, abolition, and protests against one’s own empire (Las Casas, Wilberforce) used Jesus as the measure. The historical data stacks on the same side of the folded line.

In one sentence: you judge with Christ while pretending the ruler is yours; when a Christian fails, you use that same ruler and call it a proof against Christ.

You breathe Christian air.

If you can stand in 2026 and call these things evil —

slavery,
the infant left to die,
the girl as a prize of war,
the widow on the pyre,
the gladiator killed for sport,
human sacrifice,
cannibal conquest,
the rack,
the witch-fire of the mob,
colonial plunder,
famine ignored while grain is sold,
the peasant crushed by the planter,
the foreigner treated as another species,
the king who calls himself a god —

you did not invent that verdict. You inherited it.

You breathe Christian air.

In Eden the first politics began.
Not fruit.
The right to name good and evil without God.

“You will be like God.”
That lie is the oldest heresy
and the newest fashion.
Relativism is Genesis 3 in modern clothes.

I will decide.
My age will decide.
My tribe will decide.
My desire will decide.

Man reached for the throne.
Man wrote his own law.
Man called darkness light.
And it always went wrong.

When every man did
what was right in his own eyes,
the weak became food.
History is that sentence written in blood.

Rome cheered the arena
and exposed the infant.
Slaves were tools with voices.
Glory drank death as sport.

Greece could be brilliant
and still toss a baby.
Aristotle could call some men
slaves by nature.

China could raise a magnificent court
and treat mass life as imperial clay.
Opponents buried.
The small uncounted.

Islam, as history actually ran,
regulated slavery
and did not abolish the category.
The captive girl could become property.

Pagan altars knew the child in the fire,
the heart cut out for the sun,
the widow burned,
the enemy eaten to steal his strength.

Those worlds had order.
They had ritual.
They had power.
They did not have a verdict against the strong.

Then the Word became flesh.
Not a slogan.
A Person.
The image of the invisible God.

The Lamb.
The second Adam.
He did not seize the throne as plunder.
He emptied Himself.

At the cross the old lie
was answered in public.
The Strong One became weak.
The Judge was judged.

The Holy One stood with the crushed.
Good and evil stopped being a private vote.
They were nailed to a tree
and raised where the nations could see.

Jesus is not one more teacher
in the marketplace of values.
He is the measure of what is good.
The age does not judge Him.

He judges the age.
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
Every human leaks.
Therefore every human needs a Reference that does not leak.

Christians did evil.
Say it without flinching.
Chain. Pyre. Raid. Pride.
The jar cracked in a thousand hands.

But the jar is not the water.
Spain was not the gospel.
Britain was not the Lamb.
A stamped cross is not Christ.

When you damn the Christian
for the slave ship and the whip,
the tongue in your mouth
was trained by Christ.

Rome did not teach you
that the infant is sacred.
The arena did not teach you
that spectacle-killing is shame.

The raid did not teach you
that no human is loot.
The old shrine did not teach you
that a widow is not fuel.

You inherited the accusation
and forgot the Accuser.
The standard that condemns the cracked cup
came from the living water.

Basil built a city of mercy.
Las Casas turned on his own empire.
Quakers and Wilberforce
fought the trade until the law broke.

Carey left a Sunday service
to write a ban against the pyre.
Clay people.
Clear Reference.

This is the whole story:
Eden’s grab,
the long chaos of men playing God,
then Jesus —
the only Reference that does not leak.

Do not confuse the cracked cup
with the living water.
The cup will fail you.
Jesus will not.

He is the measure of the good.
History keeps pointing back to Him.
You still breathe Christian air.
Do not pretend you made it.

If a dog loves chicken, you do not lure it with charcoal.
If a child lives for candy, you do not bait the trap with a fast.
If a thirsty man will sell his soul for wine, you do not hold out an empty cup and call it joy.
You offer what the hunger already wants. That is how you catch a creature. That is how you tell a hunter from a father.

Now put the two majority claims on that table and watch what is served.

In the days of Jesus the Jews wanted a war-king: Rome off their necks, a throne in Zion, a Messiah who wins the way men win. He offers the opposite. No legion. A cross. “My kingdom is not of this world.” The Gentiles wanted to keep the old feast—pleasure, orgies, the body as a god, even the rot of incest that Paul names in the churches’ neighbor-world. Jesus says stop. Do not look to lust. Tear out the eye. One man. One woman. Master the flesh. In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage. He is not selling chicken to the dog. He is offering charcoal to a mouth trained on meat—and then dying to make the mouth new.

In the days of Muhammad the men who built the army wanted what fighting men have always wanted: women, wine, spoil, a heaven that feels like the night after a raid. Look at the menu. Wives here. More promised there. A lawful appetite crowned. That is not charcoal. That is chicken. The lure matches the pack.

Today the world is more promiscuous, not less. The same test still works. What does each message cost the male ego now?

Then, the greatest machine of power was an army of men. A revelation that baptizes the sword and the bed will gather that machine fast. Now the greatest machine is the state: parties, courts, borders, schools, media. Jesus still says the same inconvenient sentence: his kingdom is not of this world. He will not hand you a ministry of truth to capture. He will not let you baptize your coalition and call it Zion. The gospel remains against what we like. It tells the religious nationalist he cannot have a holy empire. It tells the libertine he cannot have a holy orgy. It tells the ambitious man the last seat is a towel and a basin. So ask the honest question: if someone wanted to deceive us, would he keep offering charcoal—fasting to the sweet tooth, a cross to the man who wants a crown, one wife to the man who wants a harem, a kingdom not of this world to the man who wants this world?

And the other story: the Scriptures were “corrupted,” they say—so that what remains is the hard road. Fasting for candy-lovers. A crucified God for people who wanted a Caesar. That would be the stupidest fraud in history. Forgers who want followers do not edit the bait down. They edit it up.

Watch the present. Islam can advance inside countries where a political left that hates the church will walk beside it for a season. That left is not built on Sinai. It is built on permission: the body as politics, gender as clay, desire as a right. For a while the alliance is useful. A shared enemy—the Christ who says no. After the house is taken, the guest does not keep the host’s rules. Then comes sharia: the army under another name. If a doctrine already allows deception for the cause when the cause is threatened, the handshake was never the destination. It was the door.

So which god is hunting, and which God is fathering?

The god who plates what the age already craves—women and wine for the raider then, power and narrative for the operator now—is easy to recognize. He does not need to change the human heart. He only needs to bless it.

The God of Jesus keeps serving charcoal to the old appetite: die to yourself, one covenant bed, no orgy, no child as a prize, no throne of this world, no virgins as pay, only God. He would be a fool of a con man. He makes sense as a Father who would rather lose the crowd than feed the sickness.

Scripture was not “fixed” to make the gospel tastier. The gospel is still the least marketable offer on the table. That is how you know it was not designed by a man building an army—or a man building a government. It was designed by someone who wants sons, not customers.

In reality, the Left is nothing but the Devil's excrement. He comes along and shits his stinking filth onto nations, ruins the youth, promotes promiscuity, empties minds in favor of a sick collective, attacks families and faith, and then sends his soldiers to dominate, conquer, and enslave people so they will worship him.

text:
Start here.

A war-band can take a peninsula and still not own its own story. Muhammad died in Medina in June 632. Within a generation his men were not reciting one fixed text. According to the Sunni canon itself—Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 and 5102—Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, campaigning in Armenia and Azerbaijan under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan (r. 644–656), heard Syrian and Iraqi soldiers accusing one another over variant readings of the Qur’an and feared schism. Uthman ordered Zayd ibn Thabit and a small committee to produce one official recension from the sheets already gathered under Abu Bakr after the battle of Yamamah (c. 632–633), sent copies to the main garrison cities, and commanded that other written collections be burned. That is not how a father handles truth. That is how a commander handles a riot in camp. The man of the raid had offered fighting men what fighting men already priced—women, spoil, rank, a paradise with the smell of victory on it—and he got his army: Hijrah 622, Badr 624, the taking of Mecca in 630, a community armed enough that, after 632, it walked out of Arabia and broke the near frontiers of Byzantium and Ctesiphon. He did not get control of the wording. The sword can gather a host. It cannot keep ten mouths from rewriting the banner. When the banner starts a fight, the caliph does not repent. He lights a fire under the other pages (Bukhari 4987).

That is the method. Feed the pack. Win the ground. When the story cracks, burn the variants. A hunter plates the hunger. He does not remake it.

Now the other table.

The gospel is still the worst product in the shop. No one designing customers writes it. Someone who wants sons writes it. Soft men swollen with appetite will always walk to the louder stall. That walk is not evidence. It is the x-ray. And it leaves Jesus where He stands: above the stall, the legion, and every cheap replacement—worthy, because He refused to purchase us with our vice. He paid in blood.

God is not recruiting buyers. He is calling children home.

Jesus does not bait Jew or Greek with their favorite dish. He orders both to drop the plate.

The Jew wanted a war-crown: Rome thrown off, Zion armed, a Messiah who wins like Caesar. Jesus answers with timber and nails, under Pontius Pilate, c. 30–33. “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Come back to the Father. Receive a name. “To all who received Him, He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12).

The Gentile wanted the old night: the body as shrine, the feast that never closes, the rot Paul names in the streets around the churches (Romans 1; 1 Corinthians 5–6). Jesus answers with a cut. Stop staring. Tear out the eye (Matthew 5:27–32). One covenant bed. Rule the flesh. Then live as a son, not as a stomach.

He does not toss steak to the wolf. He puts bread in a mouth that only knew raw meat—and then dies and rises so the mouth can say Abba. No harem as wages. Adoption. The Lamb dies for the enemy. The stone rolls.

Muhammad runs the opposite shop. He wanted a host and he bought one with the inventory the host already priced: raids for caravan wealth after 622, plural marriage written into law, captives as a lawful yield of war. That raises banners. It does not raise sons of God. And when the inventory of words would not sit still, Uthman, about 650–653, burned the extras. Army first. Canon by bonfire second.

Look at what grows, without perfume. Where Christ’s gospel actually entered—not the costume of Christ, the command of Christ—even under crooked kings, a strange orchard appeared: the weak life counts, the child is not a clan chip only, the woman is not a share of loot, letters and universities sprout because a soul is addressed by God and must learn to answer. Cathedral schools and the medieval universitas—Bologna (1088), Paris (c. 1150), Oxford (c. 1096)—did not grow from a tent of captives. They grew from a Cross and from “let the little children come to Me” (Mark 10:14).

A creed built to please the raider will not pause and see woman and child as the image of God. It will see them as cargo—flesh, hush, wall. Useful falsehood, sanctified war, the killing of the holdout, poverty called fate: that is not bad weather on the map. That is what you plant when desire wears a scabbard.

If truth were the average male wish, heaven would be unemployed. We already know the wish: more body, more force, more alibi. That wish is the clay of this century—in the old paganism that still rides under a prophet’s name, and in the new ideologies that spit on the church. Both want a homemade god. One names it caliphate. One names it State. Both say the vote of man is the verdict of right. That sentence is not faith. It is apostasy with a flag.

The hunter blesses the pulse. The Father breaks it and names it child. That is why the gospel still will not sell to synagogue or forum. And that is why Jesus still has no rival: He would rather lose the crowd than nurse the fever. He lost the crowd. He kept the empty tomb. He kept the way back to the Father.

text:
LIQUIDIA $LQDA CLOSED AT $30.26. TWO PATENT CLAIMS SURVIVED:

Liquidia LQDA at $30.26, -$40.43 / -57.19% on Wednesday, and $30.16 after hours (as of 7:47pm ET), -$0.10 / -0.32% from Wednesday's close. The Morrisville, North Carolina company sells Yutrepia, a dry powder of treprostinil, a drug that widens blood vessels in the lungs. The shares were halted for pending news, then reopened into the loss. A Delaware court kept two patent claims covering one of the drug's two uses and said Yutrepia infringes them. The order that would say what has to change is not written. The shares already gave up $40.43. The evening took off another $0.10.

United Therapeutics (UTHR) at $541.89, +$60.42 / +12.55% on Wednesday, and $541.90 after hours (as of 7:44pm ET), +$0.01 / +0.00% from Wednesday's close, sells Tyvaso, its own inhaled form of the same drug, and it filed the suit. The same ruling lifted these shares. The evening added one cent. United Therapeutics is not a Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Growth, Hypergrowth, or Income name: the day is a court win for a drug already on the market, not a new climb, a discount, a growth reset, or cash just handed to owners.

The case is in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware, under the Hatch-Waxman Act, the law that lets the owner of a branded drug press a patent around a rival product. The patent is U.S. Patent No. 11,826,327. Six claims were asserted. The court kept claims 1 and 14 and threw out the other four. Liquidia described the two that survived as covering PH-ILD, high blood pressure in the lungs that comes with scarring or inflammation of the lung tissue, treated with inhaled treprostinil, including a dry powder. The two sides have until October 7 to submit a proposed judgment, the paper that states the remedy. The court did not set the day it will sign one.

The remedy, Liquidia said, could run from taking PH-ILD off the label to a wider limit on whether the product stays on the market. Roger Jeffs, the chief executive, said the company disagrees on claims 1 and 14, will appeal, and will ask the Food and Drug Administration to remove PH-ILD from the label. It cannot yet put a dollar figure on the outcome. October 7 is a proposal. An appeal comes after something is signed.

The other approved use is PAH, high blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs as its own disease. Approval for both uses came on May 23, 2025, and shipping started that June. The two claims that survived do not name PAH. The sales dollars are not split between the two uses. That missing split is the number Wednesday did not have.

Quarter ended June 30, reported August 12:

- Product sales, money from the drug: $170.4 million, up 31% from the first quarter, against $6.5 million a year earlier
- Service revenue, a profit-share on a separate generic injection: $1.3 million, against $2.3 million
- Together: $171.7 million, against $8.8 million
- Cost of product sales, the direct cost of making the drug: $10.8 million, so $159.6 million was left of product sales
- Profit: $74.7 million, or $0.74 a diluted share, which counts shares the company could still issue, against a loss of $0.49. The March quarter earned $52.9 million
- Cash: $284.2 million, against $190.7 million at December 31

At June 30 the owners' stake, what the business owns minus what it owes, was $195.1 million. Debt was $176.1 million, $54.0 million of it due within a year, so debt sits $19.0 million under the stake. On the 89.1 million shares out that day, $30.26 is about $2.70 billion, and the $40.43 drop is about $3.60 billion. Since the June 2025 launch, through July 31: about 5,900 prescriptions and more than 5,000 patients started.

The same August 12 report estimates about 45,000 PAH patients diagnosed and treated in the United States, and more than 60,000 people with PH-ILD. People are not dollars.

The ruling fell on the last day of the quarter now ending, so June cannot contain it, and September's shipments other than that day were already out. L606, a second inhaled treprostinil in a pivotal PH-ILD trial called Re-Spire, was not named. Liquidia's description of the two claims is inhaled treprostinil for that disease.

The Hypergrowth Len5 hunts very fast sales growth at a size that is already real. Liquidia is eleventh of 30 because of the launch: $171.7 million against $8.8 million, with no three-year record under it, which is what keeps it a notch behind. What would knock Liquidia off the Hypergrowth Len5: product sales well under $170.4 million after PH-ILD leaves the label, or a remedy that limits the product beyond the label. What would leave that fit in place: PAH alone still near $170.4 million. No date is set for the September report. October 7 comes first.

The June 30 books also meet the Quality Len5. That one looks for a profitable, sound business and does not need a low price. Gross profit, what is left after the direct cost, was positive. The quarter earned $74.7 million on the $195.1 million stake, and debt of $176.1 million does not exceed it. The drop did not earn this. What would knock Liquidia off the Quality Len5: debt through $195.1 million, or a quarter back at a loss.

A fall this large gets read as cheap. It is not that yet. Momentum hunts a stock climbing on real news, and $40.43 the other way is not a climb. What would put Liquidia on the Momentum Len5: the shares back above Tuesday's $70.69, still there after PAH stays on the market. Quality-Value hunts a hard-to-copy business at a discount. What would put Liquidia on the Quality-Value Len5: PAH still carrying sales near $170.4 million, at a price still near $30.26. Deep-Value and Special-Situations hunts a price below a cautious reading of what the business is worth, or an event that rewrites the math. Wednesday is the event. What would put Liquidia on the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5: a label-only judgment, and a price still near $30.26 once the PH-ILD share of $170.4 million is printed. Growth hunts rising profit the price has not already paid for. What would put Liquidia on the Growth Len5: diluted profit still near $0.74 with PH-ILD gone, shares still near $30.26. Income hunts cash paid to owners that the business can keep paying. No dividend was declared. What would put Liquidia on the Income Len5: a dividend that $74.7 million of profit still covers after the remedy.

October 7 brings a proposed order, not a signed one. Liquidia has already offered to take PH-ILD off the label. The $170.4 million is still unsplit, so the close priced either that offer or a wider order nobody has signed.

text:
THE CALORIES YOU DON'T NOTICE. 🥫🥕

"My message is clear: Eat real food." That's how Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. summed up the new Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030, released with Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins in January 2026. The guidelines call out highly processed foods and tell Americans to sharply cut refined carbohydrates.

But is "real food" just a slogan? A landmark experiment at the National Institutes of Health suggests it's much more.

🔬 In 2019, NIH researcher Kevin Hall and his team admitted 20 adults to the NIH Clinical Center, where every bite could be measured. For 2 weeks they ate an ultra-processed diet, and for 2 weeks an unprocessed diet, in random order. The clever part: both diets offered the same calories, sugar, fat, fiber, salt and protein on the plate. People could eat as much or as little as they wanted.

📊 The results:

On the ultra-processed diet, people ate 508 more calories a day.

They gained about 0.9 kg (2 pounds) in 2 weeks.

On the unprocessed diet, they lost about 0.9 kg.

The extra calories came from carbohydrates and fat, not protein.

Same people. Same nutrients offered. The only difference was how processed the food was, and their bodies simply ate more. The researchers concluded that limiting ultra-processed foods may be an effective strategy to prevent and treat obesity.

🧠 One likely reason: ultra-processed foods are soft, fast and easy to eat. They can slip past your body's "I'm full" signals before those signals have time to arrive.

Real food isn't a trend. It's how your appetite was designed to work. 🍎

📌 How to use it:
✅ Use the kitchen test: if your great-grandmother wouldn't recognize it as food, eat it less often.
✅ Build meals from single-ingredient foods: eggs, meat, fish, beans, vegetables, fruit, rice, potatoes, nuts and olive oil.
✅ Watch the "healthy" traps: flavored yogurts, cereal bars, instant oatmeal packets and bottled smoothies are often ultra-processed.
✅ Cook in batches on the weekend so real food is the easy choice on busy weekdays.
✅ Slow down: put your fork down between bites and give your fullness signals time to catch up.

How much of what you ate yesterday came in a package with more than five ingredients?

📚 Study: Hall et al., 2019 (PMID 31105044)

text:
Why Do Democrats Want Political Power?
Part 2
Chapter 1 of 3
.
Miranda: “How beauteous mankind is! O, brave new world / That has such people in’t!”
Prospero: “‘Tis new to thee.”
(Shakespeare, The Tempest, Act V, Scene 1.)
.
“We have left undone those things which we ought to have done, and we have done those things which we ought not to have done.” (The Book of Common Prayer, 1979, “Daily Morning Prayer: Rite One,” Confession of Sin, p. 41.)
.
The Book of Common Prayer offers a useful beginning for an inquiry into public policy. Its distinction is exact. Governments can injure a society by what they undertake and by what they neglect. The second category is particularly convenient for politicians: the consequences commonly arrive after the speeches have been forgotten.
.
Why do Democrats want political power? Presumably to accomplish something that would otherwise remain undone. That is the proposition to be examined. The sincerity of their concern is not the issue. The adequacy of their governing program is.
.
No question tests that adequacy more severely than global warming. Democrats have enacted substantial climate measures, notably the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. But expenditure is an instrument, and emissions reduction an intermediate objective. The ultimate question is what climate we intend to leave our children, and whether our policies can deliver it. A party asking to govern should be able to distinguish these things. (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, “New EPA Report Shows Major Emissions Reductions in Electricity Sector from President Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act,” September 12, 2023.)
.
Let us stipulate, as the lawyers say, that the United States reaches net zero. Let us improve upon this agreeable assumption and stipulate that the rest of the world does likewise. Have we then restored a safe climate? We have not. Net zero carbon dioxide is essential to arresting the long-term rise in global temperature; it does not promise a return to the temperature at which our cities, farms and coastlines developed. Sea level can continue rising for centuries:
.
The scientific consensus is that the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets are expected to lose mass faster over the next 25 to 50 years than they did during the 20th century, primarily because of continued atmospheric and ocean warming.
.
Using the approximate Miami estimates:
.
•2050: about 1 foot (30 cm) of relative sea-level rise.
•2075: about 2 feet (60 cm), with a plausible range of roughly 1.5-2.5 feet.
.
Stabilizing the temperature and undoing the damage are different undertakings. (IPCC, Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Summary for Policymakers, sections B.5 and D.1.; NASA, IPCC AR6 Sea Level Projection Tool)
.
This is the sense in which I argue that net zero is not good enough. It is a necessary achievement, but an incomplete definition of success. If the temperature at which we stabilize is itself dangerous, a government must consider how to bring it down. It must also prepare for consequences already set in motion. (“Net Zero Is Not Good Enough”; IPCC, Climate Change 2021, Summary for Policymakers, sections B.5 and D.1.)
.
James Hansen has put the matter with characteristic directness. Discussing his paper “Global Warming in the Pipeline” in November 2023, he said: “The 2°C warming limit is dead, unless we take purposeful actions to alter the earth’s energy imbalance.” His paper calls for lower greenhouse-gas emissions, international cooperation and deliberate intervention in that imbalance. Its objective is explicit: “The enormity of consequences demands a return to Holocene-level global temperature.” That is an argument for cooling the planet. (Alejandro de la Garza, “We Need Geoengineering to Stop Out of Control Warming, Warns Climate Scientist James Hansen,” TIME, November 2, 2023; James E. Hansen and colleagues, “Global Warming in the Pipeline,” Oxford Open Climate Change, November 2, 2023.)
.
Hansen’s conclusions about the necessity of solar management intervention remain disputed. However, his paper expressly says that a rapid emissions phase out could prevent most of that equilibrium warming. The best estimate for net zero carbon dioxide remains approximately stable global temperature. The responsible argument for additional action rests on the danger of the resulting climate, the possibility of further warming and the limits of reversibility. It requires no misstatement of the science. (Hansen and colleagues, “Global Warming in the Pipeline,” abstract; IPCC, Climate Change 2021, Summary for Policymakers, section D.1.)
.
Other scientists identify reasons to plan beyond the central estimate. Joeri Rogelj of Imperial College London warns that “there is a non-negligible chance that global warming will continue after net zero and intensify dangerous climate change.” A 2023 scientific review reported roughly a one-in-six chance that the additional warming could exceed 15 percent of the warming already reached. Two degrees could therefore become more than 2.3 degrees. Uncertainty of this kind should enlarge the scope of planning. It is a peculiar reason for narrowing it. (Hayley Dunning, “Emissions Plans Must Consider Risk of Global Warming Continuing after Net Zero,” Imperial College London, November 2023, reporting Sofia Palazzo Corner and colleagues, “The Zero Emissions Commitment and Climate Stabilization,” Frontiers in Science.)
.
Kyle Armour of the University of Washington identifies another complication: “This paper looks at the temporary warming that can’t be avoided.” His colleagues modeled the sudden cessation of all human emissions, including cooling aerosols as well as greenhouse gases. Because the aerosols disappear quickly, their removal produced a temporary warming of about 0.2°C, lasting roughly ten to twenty years, before subsequent cooling. And Hansen identified the same acceleration of warming with the removal of aerosols. These studies show why a policy must specify which emissions decline, how rapidly and with what near-term consequences. (Hannah Hickey, “Including All Types of Emissions Shortens Timeline to Reach Paris Agreement Temperature Targets,” University of Washington, June 6, 2022, reporting Michelle Dvorak and colleagues, Nature Climate Change; Global Warming Has Accelerated, February 3, 2025, Environment: Science and Policy for Sustainable Development, volume 67, issue 1, pages 6–44. (Hansen and coauthors, 2025 paper.))
.
The scale of the inheritance is considerable. From 1850 through 2024, humanity emitted approximately 2.73 trillion metric tons of carbon dioxide from fossil fuels, industry and land-use change. About 1.06 trillion tons of that cumulative addition remained in the atmosphere; much of the rest entered the oceans and land. Annual emissions and accumulated atmospheric pollution are different quantities. The atmosphere keeps the account even when a government changes its accounting period. (Pierre Friedlingstein and colleagues, “Global Carbon Budget 2025,” Earth System Science Data, 2026, cumulative carbon budget for 1850–2024; carbon converted to CO₂ using 44/12.)
.
Then there are tipping points. A gradual increase in temperature can produce a change that is abrupt locally and enduring thereafter. Permafrost illustrates the problem. When ground ice thaws, land can collapse into lakes, wetlands and gullies. The altered landscape changes drainage, heat transfer and the conditions under which buried organic matter decomposes. Such changes need not follow the patient pace of a legislative calendar. (Katey Walter Anthony and colleagues, “21st-Century Modeled Permafrost Carbon Emissions Accelerated by Abrupt Thaw beneath Lakes,” Nature Communications, August 15, 2018.)
.
Professor Gustaf Hugelius describes what follows: “Once you pass the permafrost’s threshold and the ice has gone and the landscape has changed, it is not going to come back for hundreds of years. On a human timescale, those systems have then effectively tipped into a system that will keep emitting carbon for decades or centuries.” A temporary excess of warming can thus leave a very durable liability. (Jonathan Watts, “The Threatening Thaw: Climate Professor on Heatwave Risks to Tipping Point of Permafrost,” The Guardian, August 20, 2026.)
.
Northern permafrost soils contain roughly 1.3–1.6 trillion metric tons of organic carbon. This is not a reservoir containing that many tons of ready-made methane. Thaw allows microbes to convert some of the organic matter into carbon dioxide and methane. The IPCC cites high-warming estimates of approximately 0.84–2.61 billion metric tons of methane released during this century, with another study estimating about 5.3 billion. These are cumulative, scenario-dependent estimates, not a prediction of one sudden discharge. (Walter Anthony and colleagues, Nature Communications, 2018; IPCC, Climate Change 2021, chapter 5, section 5.4.9.)
.
Methane has about eighty times carbon dioxide’s warming effect per unit of mass over twenty years and roughly twenty-eight times over a century. Research summarized by Walter Anthony and colleagues associated permafrost carbon emissions under a high-emissions pathway with about 0.3°C of additional warming by 2100, with an uncertainty of approximately ±0.2°C. That estimate concerns the combined carbon feedback, not methane alone. It is sufficient to make the policy point: emissions from thawing ground can add to the task of reducing emissions from human activity. (United Nations Environment Programme, “Facts about Methane”; Walter Anthony and colleagues, Nature Communications, 2018, introduction.)
.
Nepal offers a more immediate lesson in the relationship between slow deterioration to the tipping point and then sudden catastrophe. On August 26, 2026, a mass of rock and glacier ice broke from Langtang Lirung and descended into the river system, producing a destructive flood and debris flow. ICIMOD identifies thawing permafrost, fractured rock and the loss of glacier support among the conditions under investigation. The precise contribution of each remains uncertain. But the broader mechanism is well understood. As geoscientist Simon Cox told Reuters, “Climate change is generating conditions that can destabilise high-mountain rock and ice.” Decades of altered conditions can end in minutes of disaster. (ICIMOD, “Kyirong–Rasuwa Flood 2026,” scientific questions and answers; Farah Master and colleagues, “Climate Change Boosted Risk of Devastating Himalayan Flood, Experts Say,” Reuters, August 27, 2026.)
.
End Chapter 1 of 3
Why Do Democrats Want Political Power Part 2
.

INDIAN GAMBLING CASINOS THRIVE WHILE NON NATIVE CASINOS DIE

Bankruptcy threatens 850 jobs at 8 Washingtin casinos, including 2 in Tri-Cities 

Sept. 30, 2026

KENNEWICK, WA - Two Tri-Cities casinos will close or shift to new management on November 30 as their parent company winds down a complicated bankruptcy. Crazy Moose Casino in Pasco and Coyote Bob’s Roadhouse Casino in Kennewick are both subject to closure or a change in management, according to notices owner Maverick Gaming Inc. sent to Mayor Charles Grimm of Pasco and Mayor Jason McShane of Kennewick this week. 

The move comes amid a flurry of closure announcements Maverick filed with the state employment department this week under the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act or WARN. The company said it will close eight casinos that collectively employ 850, including the two in the Tri-Cities. 

Maverick will close casinos in Lakewood (Chips, Macau and Palace), Everett (Great American), Silverdale (All Star) and Yakima (Caribbean) in addition to the two in the Tri-Cities. 

Though Tri-City staff members have indicated business will reopen immediately under new owners, it was not immediately clear how that will happen. Both operate under licenses held by Maverick. 

On Wednesday, the Washington State Gambling Commission confirmed no new applications were pending for either Crazy Moose or Coyote Bob’s. Filed in 2025 Las Vegas-based Maverick, also known as RunItOneTime LLC, filed for protection from creditors in U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas on July 14, 2025. Judge Alfredo R. Perez is presiding over the case. 

The sprawling legal saga covers nearly 70 Maverick entities, including Kirkland-based Maverick Washington LLC. The Washington affiliate operates 17 of the state’s 40 public house-banked card rooms, including the two in the Tri-Cities. Coyote Bob's Roadhouse Casino is at 3014 W. Kennewick Ave. in Kennewick.  

Debt, Tribal gaming blamed In court documents, RunItOneTime officials said the bankruptcy was precipitated by the company’s large debt as well as “significant competition from Tribal casinos in their key Washington market, operational misalignments, and industry headwinds more generally.” There is no tribal casino in the Tri-Cities, though several have been proposed. 

Maverick’s closest Tribal competitors are the Wild Horse Casino and Resort, operated by the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Reservation east of Pendleton, Ore., and Legends Casino, operated by the Yakama Nation in Toppenish, near Yakima. 

Crazy Moose Casino, 510 S. 20th St., employs 137 workers, including several represented by Teamsters Local 839 in Pasco, according to a notice submitted to Pasco Mayor Charles Grimm. 

Crazy Moose, 510 S. 20th St., employs 137. The 17,500-squre-foot venue features 15 table games, as well as a card room and poker. Coyote Bob’s Roadhouse, 3014 W. Kennewick Ave., employs 68. The 5,000-square-foot casino offers 12 table games and a card room. Both serve food and both have employees represented by Teamsters Local No. 839 of Pasco. 

An official said it had not been notified of potential closures or a change in management. RuniItOneTime/Maverick leases both locations after selling them as part of a larger portfolio in 2022 to raise cash. The $110.3 million deal with Blue Owl Capital (NYSE: OWL) made the casino company a tenant in the buildings while it continued to operate the businesses.

According to court documents, RunItOneTime/Maverick stopped paying rent to Blue Owl, in April 2025. When it filed for bankruptcy a few months later, it owed Blue Owl $5.9 million. Coyote Bob's Roadhouse Casino is at 3014 W. Kennewick Ave. in Kennewick. 
 
Bankruptcy by the numbers

RunItOneTime LLC listed it has 25,000 to 50,000 creditors on its bankruptcy petition. It said it has between $100 million and $500 million in assets, and $100 million to $500 million in debts.

𝐇𝐲𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐍𝐞𝐰𝐬 – 𝐒𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟑𝟎, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔

Cooling spot demand and profit-taking are testing Bitcoin’s rally, even as institutional flows and digital-asset infrastructure continue to expand.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰

Bitcoin finished nearly flat after retreating from its recent high, leaving the market caught between a still-positive longer-term trend and weakening near-term demand. The Bull Score reached 90 out of 100, but CryptoQuant estimated that spot demand contracted by about 170,000 BTC over 30 days and growth in speculative futures demand fell 90% in 15 days; meanwhile, profit-taking increased as recent buyers held average unrealized gains of 33%. That contrast helps explain why bullish trend signals have not translated into a sustained advance. Bitcoin ETF inflows and corporate accumulation provided a counterweight, but neither removes the pressure from sellers or the market’s sensitivity to yields and inflation data. Ethereum also struggled to gain traction: despite BitMine’s substantial accumulation, ETH remained below nearby resistance as ETF inflows weakened and exchange transfers increased. Beyond prices, the day’s clearest structural theme was the continued connection of digital assets to established systems. Binance is separating crypto and stock-related account functions, while payment providers, banks and market infrastructure firms are building routes for crypto payments, tokenized deposits and ledger-based records. Regulation, meanwhile, is becoming more operationally specific, from the UK’s authorization window to Illinois’ draft transaction-tax rules.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐧𝐚𝐩𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐭

• $BTC: $83,576, -0.1%
• ETH: $2,685, +0.3%
• BNB: $768.80, +1.4%
• XRP: $1.49, -0.0%
• SOL: $118.04, -0.9%
• Sentiment: CryptoQuant’s Bull Score was 90 out of 100, although its demand measures pointed to softer spot buying and weaker speculative futures growth.
• Flows: U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $66.19 million in net inflows on September 29, extending their positive run to nine sessions and about $3.08 billion in total. Weekly crypto investment-product inflows reached $3.55 billion, led by Bitcoin at $2.52 billion and Ethereum at $702 million; Solana and XRP products drew $193 million and $92.3 million, respectively.
• Macro: August core PCE inflation was 3.0% year over year and headline PCE was 3.4%. The softer-than-expected core reading eased rate-hike expectations, though Treasury yields remained elevated and markets continued to weigh inflation and labor-market data.
𝐓𝐨𝐩 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬

𝟏. 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧’𝐬 𝐛𝐮𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡 𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐦𝐞𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐰𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐝

Bitcoin’s pullback from about $87,400 left the market with conflicting signals: CryptoQuant’s Bull Score stood at 90 out of 100 after BTC crossed its 365-day moving average, but estimated spot demand had contracted by about 170,000 BTC over 30 days. Growth in speculative futures demand fell 90% in 15 days, while recent buyers held average unrealized gains of 33%, creating an incentive to take profits. The nine-session streak of U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF inflows and renewed accumulation by some large holders offered support, but those purchases have not established that overall demand has recovered. The market is therefore testing whether new buying can absorb selling, rather than simply relying on bullish technical readings. With inflation data and yields still shaping risk appetite, a failure to hold support would make the rally more vulnerable to a deeper consolidation.

𝟐. 𝐊𝐚𝐥𝐬𝐡𝐢’𝐬 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐦𝐛𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐜𝐫𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐲

Kalshi is in advanced talks to raise about $1 billion at a valuation near $40 billion, after raising $1 billion at a $22 billion valuation in May; the new financing remains unsettled, with Sequoia Capital and Wellington Management among investors reportedly discussing a leading role. The proposed valuation comes as the prediction-market platform’s activity grows, but the company is also facing questions about repeated trading in Ether perpetual contracts and the role of trading incentives. Kalshi filed to end its Volume Incentive Program no earlier than October 13, without stating a reason or linking the decision to scrutiny of its trading patterns. The CFTC is investigating trades through an account linked to former Representative Adam Kinzinger, while a separate House inquiry has expanded to other prediction-market platforms. Those are distinct proceedings, not proof of wrongdoing by Kalshi. Together, however, they put the sustainability and oversight of prediction-market growth in focus just as the company seeks a much higher valuation.

𝟑. 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐛𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐙𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡’𝐬 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐞𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐩𝐨𝐨𝐥

Funds linked to Bitget’s September 24 breach, which resulted in about $387.5 million in unauthorized transfers, were moved into Zcash’s shielded Ironwood pool, making subsequent transactions harder to trace. Investigators tracked about 2,746 ZEC, worth roughly $3.9 million, entering the pool across three transfers; the movement is part of a broader effort to route stolen assets across wallets and chains. Bitget has restored withdrawals for Bitcoin, Ether and USDT and says customer balances are protected, while the exchange works to resume other services and trace the funds. It has also reported rebuilding its Protection Fund to more than $300 million, although recovery of the stolen assets remains uncertain. The incident underscores a practical tension: cross-chain services and privacy pools can complicate tracing, while efforts by decentralized networks to block suspicious transfers raise questions about who has authority to intervene.

𝟒. 𝐔𝐊 𝐜𝐫𝐲𝐩𝐭𝐨 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐨𝐰 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬

The UK Financial Conduct Authority opened applications on September 30 for firms seeking authorization under a regime due to take effect on October 25, 2027. Covered firms should submit valid applications by February 28, 2027, to allow time for decisions before the regime begins. Existing registration under the Money Laundering Regulations will not automatically qualify a firm, and applying does not guarantee approval; businesses must identify the permissions they need and meet standards covering governance, customer protection, custody, technology and market conduct. Eligible firms that apply on time may continue specified services while their applications are assessed, while late applicants may face tighter limits. The opening of the process gives firms a clearer timetable, but it also makes authorization a concrete operational requirement rather than a distant policy discussion.

𝟓. 𝐁𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐜𝐫𝐲𝐩𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤-𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬

Binance began a staged change to move non-stock crypto assets from Funding Accounts into Spot Accounts, with the migration running through January 2027. Funding Accounts are due to be renamed Stocks Accounts in January 2027 and will primarily handle stock and stock-option settlements, with a limited set of supported settlement assets. Binance says the transition does not alter the total value of user assets and is an internal account-structure change, not a sale or liquidation. Related services are also being adjusted, including Binance Card, gift cards, Pay, and Convert, while the timing of individual balance migrations will vary. Users may need to review settings tied to Funding Accounts, such as recurring payments or Convert preferences. The redesign reflects Binance’s effort to create distinct accounting and settlement paths as its tokenized stock products expand.

𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 & 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐲

The regulatory thread is shifting from broad debate toward specific authorization, tax and oversight questions. In the UK, the FCA has opened its application process for a regime scheduled to begin on October 25, 2027, with a February 28, 2027 deadline for firms seeking time to have applications assessed before commencement. In Illinois, draft rules for a 0.2% digital-asset transaction tax are open for comment through October 30; the proposal treats stablecoins as taxable while excluding NFTs, and its treatment of DeFi depends partly on whether a platform collects qualifying fees. The CFTC has also sent proposed rules on event contracts to the White House for review, including one that would classify them as swaps and another that would exclude casino-style gambling products from that definition. Those proposals do not settle the dispute between federal and state authority, but they show that prediction markets are moving closer to formal rulemaking. Taken together, the developments point to more detailed obligations around access, classification and transaction handling, even as the boundaries of oversight remain contested.

𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 & 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤

The Bitget breach remains the day’s most immediate operational warning: funds linked to the theft entered Zcash’s shielded pool, where tracing later movements is harder, while the exchange continues restoring services and pursuing recovery. The incident also exposed disagreement over how decentralized protocols should respond to suspected stolen assets, since intervention can aid recovery but may raise questions about control and decentralization. Separately, Apple’s emergency updates addressed a CoreGraphics vulnerability that could allow code execution through a malicious file, and Apple said it may have been exploited in sophisticated attacks against selected users. SlowMist urged users handling crypto to update affected devices and avoid suspicious files, links and apps. The incidents point to different failure points–exchange withdrawal controls, cross-chain laundering and device software–so custody protections alone do not remove the need to keep wallets and devices current and verify the systems used to access funds.

𝐀𝐥𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐬 & 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐬

Altcoin performance remained uneven, matching a market where interest has broadened but selling pressure is also rising. Altcoin spot volume was reported at four times Bitcoin’s, and altcoins reached 41% of futures open interest, while deposits to exchanges surged 160% between September 14 and 28–evidence of both strong activity and potential readiness to sell. Ethereum’s institutional story was supported by BitMine’s continued accumulation, but ETH remained below nearby resistance as ETF demand weakened. Infrastructure development offered a steadier counterpoint: Cosmos Labs introduced a way to connect bank core systems with Swift’s planned blockchain-based ledger, while Ripple and CSD BR began mirroring selected Brazilian fund ownership records on the XRP Ledger without replacing the regulated ownership database. On the application side, DogeOS opened a public testnet for an EVM-compatible layer using DOGE for fees, although it has not set a mainnet date and its current security model has limitations. These projects broaden the range of financial and application uses being tested, but they are not yet equivalent to proven demand for their associated tokens.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐖𝐚𝐭𝐜𝐡

• October 13: Kalshi’s filing sets this as the earliest date for ending its Volume Incentive Program.
• October 16: Pi Network’s Protocol 28 is scheduled for Mainnet, following its Testnet deployment.
• October 27–28: The Federal Reserve’s meeting is a focus for markets weighing whether rates will be held or raised; prediction-market odds remain sentiment measures, not a policy commitment.
• October 28: Strategy shareholders are scheduled to vote on recording dividends on preferred securities daily.
• October 30: Public comments close on Illinois’ draft digital-asset transaction-tax rules.
• November 5: Zcash developers are tentatively targeting this date for the NU7 mainnet upgrade, subject to test-network results.
• November 9: The European Central Bank’s digital-euro innovation initiative closes applications at 17:00 CET.
• November 9: ConConAI’s presale is scheduled to end.
• November 12: ConConAI has planned a Uniswap v3 launch, subject to its stated schedule.
• February 28, 2027: Deadline for UK crypto firms seeking authorization ahead of the new regime.
• April 9, 2027: Australia’s separate digital-assets framework is scheduled to take effect.

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Thursday, September 30, 1976, Braniff International announced that a significant change in the stylish Airline's public contact personnel uniforms would take place. America's very own Haute Couturier Roy Halston Frowick, known simply as Halston, would replace the legendary Italian designer The Marchese de Barsento Emilio Pucci, who had been styling Braniff's uniforms since the summer of 1965. Whereas Pucci celebrated the era of freedom of expression and offered a brash style in the 1960s and 1970s, Halston would usher in an era of elegance and sophistication at Braniff International for the remainder of the 1970s and the beginning of the new decade.

Braniff became the first airline to commission a full collection by Halston who first created a new collection of uniforms for the carrier's flight attendants. These new fashions were scheduled to debut during the first part of 1977, followed by a full collection for Braniff's ground and maintenance personnel including ticket agents, cargo service personnel and maintenance technicians.

Executive Vice President Russell Thayer noted that while Halston was asked to create fashions for all of Braniff's uniformed personnel, he would also assist in designing the Airline's new look, which would include a new aircraft paint scheme. Mr. Thayer stated that, "Halston's design success and acceptance in every new field he has entered will provide wide latitude in considering what additional projects he might undertake for the airline.”

Halston, only 44-years old, was born in Evansville, Indiana, on April 23, 1932, had already dressed some of the most famous women in the world including Mary Wells Lawrence, wife of Braniff Chairman Harding L. Lawrence. He created a stunning green velvet wedding smock for Mrs. Lawrence's marriage to Mr. Lawrence in November 1967. In addition to Mrs. Lawrence, Halston also designed for the remarkably talented Liza Minelli, Lauren Bacall and America's First Lady Mrs. Jacqueline Bouvier Kennedy.

Halston began his career as a hat designer when he began selling his hats in Chicago, Illinois, beginning in 1953. His customers were a cavalcade of the rich and famous including the first lady of Hollywood gossip Mrs. Hedda Hopper and Silver Screen legend Gloria Swanson. In 1961, he designed the famous pill box hat that Mrs. Jacqueline Kennedy wore to the inauguration of her husband, John F. Kennedy. Halston continued to rise in the fashion world thanks to his impressive designs that had been noticed by the biggest fashion publications.

Once hats were no longer in fashion, Halston turned to dressmaking on a full time basis. He designed the world's first Ultrasuede shirt dress and in 1975 he created his first men's line of clothing. By 1976, Halston had established himself as America's premier fashion designer. Vogue magazine wrote in September 1976, that, "One reason American women flock to Halston is that he fills in all the gaps - in a scarce coat year, he'll do a collection of wonderful coats." Vogue also noted that regardless of the styles that were current at the time Halston went above and beyond by addressing each and every possible nuance of the latest designs, leaving nothing out.

Cosmopolitan stated that, "This forty-four year old kid from the Midwest has revived Classicism in clothes - the uncluttered, uncontrived dress in free-flowing, often multi-layered fabrics of lush comfort: cashmere, silk, chiffon and Ultrasuede." Halston created the famous Ultrasuede concept and its moniker would be given to Braniff for its new Ultra color schemes that were introduced in the summer of 1978 to rave reviews.

Photo: Braniff International Boeing 747SP-27 Coach Class was no stranger to the elegance of Braniff’s Ultra Service, which always included gourmet cuisine from around the world in both First Class and Coach. The Braniff Flight Attendant is wearing her Ivory Serving Smock over her H Blouse and Skirt, which were designed by Haute Couturier Halston.

$100,000 Drained From Bank Accounts At Wells Fargo, Bank of America and Other US Banks in One US County, Say Police – Here’s How:

Authorities just issued a new warning about a bank scam that’s hitting accounts across the US.

Police outside Washington, D.C. say customers at Wells Fargo, Bank of America, PNC and other US banks living have lost approximately $100,000 to bank impostor scams this year alone.

That’s in just one corner of the US – Prince George’s County, Maryland.

Thieves are impersonating major lenders, sending texts about suspicious account activity to trick victims into replying or calling a fake number, reports NBC4 Washington.

Victims are then instructed to withdraw money and deposit it into ATMs, or gift cards to “secure” their accounts.

Police advise people to call their bank directly using the number on their card, visiting a branch in person and hang up if anyone urges you to move money.

The FTC says such scams are on the rise, triggering $470 million in losses last year alone, commonly involving fake package deliveries, job offers and wrong number schemes.

That number is five times higher than what was reported in 2027, although the number of overall reports declined.

The FTC recommends forwarding suspicious texts to 7726 to report them.
