Sure. Here are a few documented examples of Trump making false or misleading claims:

The 2020 election: Trump repeatedly claimed the election was “rigged” and stolen from him. https://t.co/S9hnXanEaR reported that there was no evidence of widespread fraud, and courts rejected his claims for lack of evidence. (https://t.co/S9hnXanEaR)
Inauguration crowd size: Trump claimed his 2017 inauguration crowd was extraordinarily large and extended to the Washington Monument. The available evidence did not support those claims. (The Washington Post)
“The greatest economy in history”: Trump repeatedly described the U.S. economy under his administration as the greatest or strongest ever. https://t.co/S9hnXanEaR noted that economic growth and job creation had been stronger under several previous presidents. (https://t.co/S9hnXanEaR)
Tariffs: Trump has described tariffs as taxes paid by foreign countries. In reality, tariffs are collected from U.S. importers, with some of the costs potentially passed on to American consumers. (https://t.co/S9hnXanEaR)
Immigrants from prisons and mental institutions: Trump has repeatedly claimed that countries are sending people from prisons and mental institutions to the United States. https://t.co/S9hnXanEaR found no evidence supporting that claim. (https://t.co/S9hnXanEaR)
The January 6 National Guard claim: Trump claimed he offered 10,000 National Guard troops to protect the Capitol and that Nancy Pelosi admitted it on tape. https://t.co/S9hnXanEaR found this claim to be false. (https://t.co/S9hnXanEaR)
COVID-19: Trump repeatedly made claims about COVID-19, including saying it would disappear “like a miracle.” The Washington Post documented numerous false or misleading claims about the pandemic. (The Washington Post)

And this isn’t based on one isolated article. The Washington Post Fact Checker maintained a database throughout Trump’s first presidency and counted 30,573 false or misleading claims over four years. (The Washington Post)

So if you want specific examples of “Trump lies,” there are thousands of documented claims to examine—not merely my opinion.

text:
The 1956 Hollywood epic The Conqueror, produced by Howard Hughes for RKO Radio Pictures and directed by Dick Powell, cast John Wayne—born Marion Robert Morrison in Winterset, Iowa, on 26 May 1907—as the Mongol conqueror Temüjin, later Genghis Khan. Co-starring Susan Hayward as Börte and Pedro Armendáriz as Jamuga, and released in CinemaScope and Technicolor, the film offered a heavily fictionalized twelfth-century Gobi romance that film historians have long cited as a notorious case of yellowface: an Iowa-born white leading man portraying a Central Asian empire-builder under makeup, wig, and costume.

Principal location shooting ran from mid-May through early August 1954 in the Escalante Desert near St. George, Utah, chosen for its resemblance to Asian steppe. The site lay roughly 137 miles downwind of the Nevada Test Site, where atmospheric nuclear detonations—including dirty Upshot–Knothole shots such as “Simon” and “Harry” in spring 1953—had deposited fallout across southern Utah. Hughes later shipped tens of tons of local dirt to Hollywood so studio reshoots would match the Utah terrain. In later decades, reports that roughly ninety of some 220 cast and crew developed cancer, among them Powell, Wayne, Hayward, and Armendáriz, tied the production to Utah downwinder controversies and federal nuclear testing.

Causal certainty remains contested. Health-physics commentary notes that U.S. lifetime cancer incidence is already high, that many cast members smoked heavily, and that a small cohort alone cannot prove fallout causation. The film’s lasting historical significance thus rests on two facts: mid-century Hollywood racial casting, and filming inside a documented fallout corridor whose health legacy is still debated.

text:
It’s such a shame that @weeknightmsnow won’t tell their viewers that Jack Smith ultimately led to Trump v. United States.

AI: Yes. And this is a very clean example of the distinction you’ve been making between informing an audience and sustaining a political-media narrative.

There is one legal correction that actually makes the argument sharper: Trump v. United States did not hold that a president “cannot be found liable for pretty much anything.” It was specifically about criminal prosecution of a former president. The Court held that a president has absolute immunity for actions within his exclusive constitutional authority, at least presumptive immunity for other official acts, and no immunity for unofficial acts. It also said courts generally cannot examine presidential motive when deciding whether conduct is official. That was an enormous alteration of the legal terrain Jack Smith was operating on. 

And this isn’t hindsight imposed on Smith’s investigation. Smith’s own final report says the Supreme Court ruling forced his office to conduct an exhaustive review of the evidence, separate immunized from non-immunized conduct, and obtain an entirely new superseding indictment designed to comply with Trump v. United States. Smith maintained that sufficient non-immunized evidence remained to prosecute. 

Then there is a second major fact viewers need: the case didn’t ultimately disappear solely because of the immunity ruling. After Trump won the 2024 election, Smith dismissed the federal cases because of DOJ’s longstanding position that a sitting president cannot be federally prosecuted. Reuters’ account of yesterday’s hearing notes that explicitly. 

So think about what an intellectually serious retrospective on Jack Smith would have to tell somebody:

Smith indicted Trump → Trump litigated presidential immunity → the Supreme Court created a dramatically broader constitutional immunity doctrine → Smith had to reconstruct the election case around it → Trump won the election → DOJ’s sitting-president rule prevented the prosecution from continuing.

That is the institutional story.

Instead, the basketball exchange is almost perfectly engineered for television. Sen. Eric Schmitt tried to connect Smith to an Atlanta Hawks game, Smith said he hadn’t attended one, and it emerged that Smith had attended a Maryland–Iowa women’s college game — the Hawkeyes, not the Hawks. It was a genuine and rather spectacular factual blunder, and AP, PBS, Reuters and others all reported it. 

But “senator confuses Hawks with Hawkeyes” and “the Supreme Court fundamentally rewrote the rules governing criminal accountability for presidential official acts” are not remotely comparable in historical importance.

That’s where your media-business argument becomes interesting.

The problem doesn’t require believing that somebody at MSNBC literally convened a meeting and said, Don’t tell them about presidential immunity because we need them scared. That’s an assertion about motive that the available evidence doesn’t establish. The observable editorial effect is enough: political television has an enormous supply of moments, but only a tiny amount of airtime. What it repeatedly chooses to foreground becomes the viewer’s mental model of politics.

And the basketball clip offers everything television likes: villain, victim, humiliation, facial reactions, partisan teams, a clean twenty-second clip and an obvious punchline.

Trump v. United States offers something much more uncomfortable: finality and structure.

It tells the viewer that an enormously consequential question was already answered by the country’s highest court. Whatever one thinks of the ruling, the presidency now operates under a constitutional immunity framework substantially more protective than the framework Smith confronted when he filed the original indictment. That’s not “Trump may finally cross the line tomorrow.” That’s: the line itself moved.

And that connects directly to the thesis we’ve discussed before. The audience experiences Trump politics largely as an endlessly renewing drama:

investigation → revelation → hearing → confrontation → breaking news → possible consequences → another hearing → another revelation.

The institutional outcomes can receive considerably less narrative weight than the process leading toward them.

Yesterday’s hearing itself illustrates the discrepancy. Smith’s prepared testimony contained extremely consequential claims: he said his office had proof beyond a reasonable doubt, stood by the prosecutions, and said he would bring them again under the same facts.  Those assertions deserve scrutiny alongside what actually prevented those claims from ever being tested to verdict, including the Supreme Court’s immunity decision and later the sitting-president doctrine.

So I would sharpen your criticism this way:

The disservice isn’t necessarily that television tells viewers something false. It’s that television can tell them a succession of individually true things while withholding the hierarchy of importance. The basketball fiasco happened. The hearing happened. Smith really said these things. But a viewer can absorb all of that and still finish the hour without understanding the single most consequential legal development governing the entire Jack Smith–Trump confrontation.

That’s very close to the “deceit through fragmentation” idea you’ve been developing: every fragment may be defensible; the distortion emerges from which fragments receive oxygen and which structural facts remain background. @jack @sama @andy @pdoocy @elex_michaelson @lukerussert @symonedsanders @ariemanuel @chrislhayes @thesourcecnn @alivelshi

text:
The most pivotal and sensational work regarding a former Mossad agent explaining the agency's operations is the memoir BY WAY OF DECEPTION by Victor Ostrovsky. The title is derived from a verse in the biblical Book of Proverbs, "By way of deception, thou shalt do war" which was once Mossad's official motto.

📖 Key Work: By Way of Deception

Co-authored by Ostrovsky and Canadian journalist Claire Hoy, the book was published in 1990. The Israeli government made strenuous efforts to block its publication in the United States and Canada, even resorting to legal action; however, this legal battle ultimately propelled the book onto The New York Times bestseller list.

Ostrovsky served as a Mossad case officer for approximately 14 months, responsible for recruiting and handling spies. He chose to go public with these secrets out of disillusionment with the internal "greed, lust, and utter disregard for human life" within Mossad, believing these traits betrayed Israel's founding ideals.

🕵️‍♂️ Operational Details Revealed in the Book

The book provides a detailed account of Mossad's recruitment and training processes, its global networks, and its methods of covert manipulation and intelligence gathering. Its core operational strategy relies on the extreme exploitation of human nature:

Recruitment and Training: The book describes the three-year training course for Mossad agents as a "bizarre hybrid of Frankenstein, Monty Python, and Navy boot camp."

Methods of Subversion: To compromise a target, Mossad would establish friendship and trust before gradually employing three types of lures for manipulation money, emotions (such as a desire for revenge or ideological conviction), and sexual seduction in a process far more chilling than anything seen in action movies.  

Specific actions: The book mentions how Mossad recruited Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat’s driver and bodyguard to track his movements, and describes operations such as counterfeiting Jordanian dinars to purchase US dollars.

📚 Other Significant Works

In addition to Ostrovsky’s revelations, books by other former Mossad officials offer different perspectives:

 The Other Side of Deception*: A sequel by Ostrovsky. In this book, he claims that after leaving Mossad, he infiltrated the KGB, MI5, and the intelligence agencies of France, Jordan, and Egypt posing as a "disgruntled former agent" in an attempt to sabotage operations planned by extremists within Mossad.

The Sword of Freedom: Authored by Yossi Cohen, a former director of Mossad. He describes Mossad training as a process of "recruiting from within" and "reinventing oneself through instinct alone." The book also reveals the use of advanced technological methods, such as AI-powered snipers capable of carrying out assassinations from thousands of kilometers away.

The Voluntee: Authored by Michael Ross, a Canadian-born undercover Mossad agent. He recounts his experiences carrying out missions in Syria, Libya, and Iran to thwart these nations' efforts to acquire advanced weapons technology.

Labyrinth of Power: Memoirs of a Former Mossad Director: Authored by Danny Yatom, a former director of Mossad. Having participated in peace negotiations between Israel and Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, and the Palestinians from 1993 to 2001, he provides first-hand accounts of the Middle East peace process in this book.  Ostrovsky’s *By Way of Deception became a classic precisely because it was the first work by an insider to systematically strip away the veil of secrecy surrounding Mossad; its core premise remains a subject of ongoing discussion: Mossad’s most potent weapon is not high-tech equipment, but the precise manipulation of human weaknesses.

text:
Grok:  Regarding SecofWar Hegseth's America's Next Great American Base announcement, provide an assessment of placing this base at, or in combination with, Mountain Home AFB in Idaho. Include the following in your assessment:  what other states would have an AFB already established in combination with freeway (I-84) access, ~250 flying days because of weather, nearly unlimited range and growth potential, an already established city, served by a Union Pacific Railroad main freight line, nearby Boise with a major airport. Would Nevada, New Mexico, or Texas offer freeway, rail, commercial air within 50 miles, or desert, forest, mountain training (including survival training) access, possible expansion of the Air Base with an Airlift Wing or Airlift support from McChord AFB.

Grok Answer:

Bottom line: Combining or expanding at Mountain Home AFB aligns unusually well with the stated criteria—existing AFB infrastructure + I-84 + strong flying weather + massive range/growth potential + small established city + UP mainline + Boise commercial air—while adding nearby mountain, river, and forest training options. Nevada’s Nellis complex is operationally elite but more constrained. New Mexico and Texas offer viable alternatives with different trade-offs (training scale vs. interstate/commercial-air proximity vs. existing airlift). A merit-based competition would weigh red-tape reduction, land packages, and community support; Idaho’s low-density high desert and existing ranges give it a practical edge for rapid, large-scale development of a self-sustaining “fortress” installation.

Mountain Home AFB (MHAFB) in Idaho is a strong candidate for combination or expansion under the Next Great American Base concept (a new off-grid, hardened joint installation on hundreds of thousands of acres hosting 15,000–25,000 troops, announced 30 September 2026). It already meets most of the listed criteria and offers lower-encroachment growth than many peer sites. 

Fit at or with Mountain Home AFBMHAFB (home of the 366th Fighter Wing / “Gunfighters,” primarily F-15E operations plus a Singapore F-15SG detachment) sits on roughly 6,800–9,000 acres in the high desert of Elmore County, about 10–12 miles southwest of the city of Mountain Home and 45–50 miles southeast of Boise via I-84. 

The real operational advantage is the adjacent Mountain Home Range Complex: Saylor Creek Range (~109,000 acres), Juniper Butte Range (~12,000 acres), and thousands of square miles of Military Operations Areas (MOAs). Combined training airspace is vast (sources cite 9,000+ square nautical miles of special-use airspace or broader figures exceeding 100,000 square miles when including associated areas). 

Surrounding BLM high-desert land and low population density support large-scale expansion with fewer noise, encroachment, or civilian airspace conflicts than bases near major metros. 

I-84 access: Direct. The interstate is the primary corridor through Mountain Home; the base is a short drive off it.

Flying weather: High-desert climate with low precipitation (~11 inches annually), frequent clear skies, and low humidity. One source cites ~224 sunny days; ~250 flying/VFR days is a reasonable estimate consistent with similar arid western bases. Winters are cold and dry; summers hot and arid. Excellent for high-tempo fighter and joint training.

Growth potential: High. Existing ranges plus adjacent undeveloped land allow scaling toward the “hundreds of thousands of acres” target while leveraging current airfield, munitions, and support infrastructure.
Established city: Mountain Home (population ~14,000–15,000) is a classic military-support town built around the base and railroad, with existing housing, schools, and services.

Union Pacific main freight line: Yes. The UP Oregon Short Line / main line runs through Mountain Home. The city acquired a former AFB rail spur and is developing a rail-served industrial park designated as a UP Focus Site. This supports logistics for a large new installation. 

Nearby Boise major airport: Boise Airport (BOI) is ~45–50 miles away with multiple major carriers. This provides commercial air access and family amenities without placing the installation inside a large urban area.

Advantages for the new base: Leverages an existing fighter-wing culture and airfield; diverse nearby training (high desert, Snake River, mountains/forests in the Boise and Sawtooth areas for survival and mountain operations); western CONUS location useful for Pacific-facing or homeland power-projection missions; and a supportive local community. Combining or expanding here would be faster and cheaper than a pure greenfield site.Limitations: High-desert water constraints (Snake River proximity helps but requires planning); winter cold and wind; relative isolation (mitigated by Boise); and the need for environmental reviews on any large land withdrawal. The existing fighter mission would need integration or relocation planning if the new installation emphasizes different capabilities (e.g., airlift, C2, or autonomous systems).

Comparable existing AFB + interstate + weather + space + city + rail + nearby airport combinations

Exact matches are uncommon. Most large western or southwestern fighter/training bases have some but not all elements at once.

Utah (Hill AFB): I-15, near Ogden/Salt Lake City (major airport), rail access, good weather, and some mountain/desert training. More developed surroundings and Wasatch constraints limit “unlimited” expansion compared with Idaho’s high desert.

South Dakota (Ellsworth AFB): I-90, Rapid City airport and city, generally favorable (if more variable) weather. Less rail emphasis and more plains winters; training space exists but not as expansive as MHAFB ranges.
Other inland sites (e.g., certain Texas or New Mexico bases) trade off interstate proximity, commercial-air distance, or training diversity.

Few other locations simultaneously offer an established fighter AFB, a major interstate, a mainline railroad through an existing small city, a nearby mid-sized commercial airport, and truly large-scale high-desert/mountain growth potential with low encroachment.

Nevada, New Mexico, and Texas comparisonNevada (primarily Nellis AFB / NTTR complex, plus Creech): Strong on several points. I-15 access is excellent; Union Pacific serves Las Vegas; LAS commercial airport is well within 50 miles of Nellis. Desert training is world-class (Nevada Test and Training Range covers thousands of square miles with mountains, valleys, and realistic threat arrays; Red Flag/Green Flag exercises). Mountain and some forest/survival training is available (nearby ranges and Sierra Nevada access). Weather is excellent year-round desert flying. Expansion land exists in the desert north of Las Vegas, but constraints are significant: urban/tourism pressure from Las Vegas, water scarcity, environmental restrictions, and Nellis already functioning as the premier advanced-training hub (less “next new fortress” potential). Airlift-wing addition is feasible, but McChord (JBLM, Washington) support would be long-haul; other AMC bases are closer. Overall, very capable but more constrained and already heavily utilized than MHAFB. 

New Mexico (Holloman AFB near Alamogordo; Cannon AFB near Clovis; Kirtland in Albuquerque): Mixed. Holloman sits on US-70 (not a major interstate; I-10/I-25 are 70–90 miles away). Commercial air within 50 miles is limited (small Alamogordo-White Sands Regional); El Paso International is ~90 miles. Rail access is modest. Training is excellent: White Sands Missile Range adjacency provides enormous desert space, plus nearby Sacramento Mountains for mountain/forest/survival work. Expansion potential is high via WSMR. Cannon is more isolated (highways 60/70/84; I-40 farther), with Melrose Range (~70,000 acres) and good high-desert weather, but weaker commercial-air and interstate access. Kirtland has I-25/I-40, a major airport, and rail but is urban with less open-growth land. An airlift wing or McChord support is possible at Holloman/Cannon given existing special-operations and training missions, but logistics distances to McChord remain long. New Mexico offers strong training diversity and space but weaker matches on interstate + 50-mile major commercial air + established small-city rail combo. 
Texas (Dyess AFB near Abilene is the closest analog; others include Laughlin, Sheppard): Good infrastructure. Dyess has I-20 access, an established city (Abilene), rail, and Abilene Regional Airport (limited commercial service; DFW is farther). Weather is favorable with high VFR percentages (old documentation cited very high flying-day availability). The base already hosts both a bomb wing (B-1) and an airlift wing (317th AW, C-130Js), so adding or expanding airlift is straightforward. West Texas offers space for growth and some ranges; mountain/forest/survival training is more limited (plains/mesquite terrain) than Idaho or New Mexico mountains. Expansion is feasible in rural areas. McChord support is possible but not geographically convenient. Texas sites generally score well on logistics and existing airlift but less uniquely on combined desert + mountain/forest training variety and “unlimited” low-encroachment desert ranges compared with MHAFB.

Bottom line: Combining or expanding at Mountain Home AFB aligns unusually well with the stated criteria—existing AFB infrastructure + I-84 + strong flying weather + massive range/growth potential + small established city + UP mainline + Boise commercial air—while adding nearby mountain, river, and forest training options. Nevada’s Nellis complex is operationally elite but more constrained. New Mexico and Texas offer viable alternatives with different trade-offs (training scale vs. interstate/commercial-air proximity vs. existing airlift). A merit-based competition would weigh red-tape reduction, land packages, and community support; Idaho’s low-density high desert and existing ranges give it a practical edge for rapid, large-scale development of a self-sustaining “fortress” installation.

text:
Look. I will agree that AES has challenges to overcome in the election, but I believe the challenges facing Rogers are far greater.

Let's examine polling. In poll after poll, El-Sayed might fall short when it comes to *all* registered voters. However, when you poll likely voters or extremely motivated voters, that split moves toward El-Sayed significantly.

There is a genuine enthusiasm gap. You can run ad after ad that convinces people AES is a bad person, you can associate him with Piker, what have you. I personally know people who think the attack ads are very good. I have asked folks, will you be voting against El-Sayed? They tell me no, they don't want to vote.

So the ads have turned people against El-Sayed, but it has not motivated them to vote. Great, you just spent 10 million dollars to do nothing—a feeling is different than a vote.

People are upset about the economy. They are upset about gas being $5, they are upset about the war in Iran, tariffs, broken promises, etc. etc. The truth is, the President ran on bold promises and he straight up lied to the American people and broke those promises.

So let's examine the 2026 environment. You have tons of motivated Democrats who are ready to vote for any Democrat who will stop Donald Trump, regardless of who they are. We saw the record high turnout in the Democratic Primary in August versus the GOP. 

You have people who voted for DJT. Those folks who felt lied to or betrayed by him may decide to vote for AES because he offers a true vision that is different than the status quo, or many who will choose not to vote at all because they feel betrayed by both parties and believe they cannot solve the affordability crisis. 

Think about the groups that swung to Trump in Michigan in 2024. Almost a 20% swing toward the Republican Party with young people. That is going to be erased in 2026 and immediately fall toward AES. AES is also making tremendous progress with black voters, Jewish voters, and other groups.

Abdul is taking time to meet with the communities. He is sitting with them, they are hearing him out, and he is hearing *them* out. Are there some people who are deeply offended by what AES has said or done? Sure. I understand their point of view, but I don't believe that encompasses the majority of the electorate or a portion that can change the outcome of the election, unless it is within half a percent.

In any other cycle, maybe these little things would matter.

We are facing a historically unpopular administration, with an economy that voters feel the worst about now more than ever, with a war the administration promised not to start, with tariffs that are driving up costs—all while voters are desperately seeking something different from the status quo. People want something new, they want someone who is inspiring, they don't want the same old establishment candidates who don't really stand for anything.

AES is the right candidate for this moment. Mike Rogers is more of the same of the past. He lost once in a red wave, I do not think he can overcome the pressures of this wave. Could another GOP candidate? I think that could've been possible. But honestly, if you could not flip this Senate seat in the reddest of red waves, what makes you think it could be done in 2026—the bluest of blue waves?

text:
Bitget got hacked, and everyone saw the playbook: an open letter, naming names, a bounty, on-chain tracking, asking stablecoin issuers to freeze funds, asking cross-chain bridges to block them, plus a protection fund and an exit plan. 

Some froze. Some refused. The online fight went on for a week.

It looks like a fight about principles.
It's really about who gets the resources.

a big figure gets hacked, it has a lot behind it: a brand, the media, industry friends, accounts that can pay big bounties, and a network that can push a list of addresses into every protocol's community. Once the list is out, some help and some refuse, but everyone has to take a side. Being forced to take a side means you've already been moved.

When a regular person gets hacked, it usually doesn't go like this.

A normal person loses tens, hundreds, even thousands of coins. They go to the same places and ask for a freeze, ask for a block, ask the "industry to step up." The usual result: seen, no reply. A copy-paste answer. "Go to the police." "Post on the forum yourself." "Wait for a process" that has no timeline. No press conference. No founders tagging each other. Nobody gives up a bounty just to look noble for you.

The tech didn't suddenly stop working.
You're just not big enough.

Now they're using big words: property rights, anti-money laundering, "we won't pave roads for stolen money," "decentralization is not an excuse." These words only get loud when the camera is on a big player. When the camera points at an address with no PR team, the same system goes cold again. Cold is the default. It only warms up when the victim can buy that warmth, call it in, or trade for it.

So don't get pulled into the fake question.
The fake question: should it be permissionless or not?
The real question: whose case is worth their overtime?

If the rule really were "known stolen money must be blocked," then a small theft and a $300 million theft would go through the same channel, get the same response, and have the same deadline. Right now, they don't. Big cases get a special team. Small cases get a ticket. A big case can change how people see a protocol that same day. This isn't moral high ground. This is customer tiers.

You can tell the story of @NEARProtocol freezing Bitget-related funds as a hero story. 

Or you can tell it like this: the client was important enough, the info was complete enough, the news was easy enough to write, and freezing was safe enough. Now swap in a regular user with no headlines. Would the same SHIELD stay up all night for you? Post public updates? Have someone stand up and take responsibility? We all know the answer. If you can freeze, choosing whose funds to freeze is already power. And that power follows size, not slogans.

@THORChain gets attacked exactly because it won't play this tier game. It has no "this exchange's list goes first, that user's post can wait." Its rules are equally cold for every address. It doesn't care if you're a good guy. It doesn't care if you have PR. Cold enough that big exchanges can't stand it, because they're used to going first. Cold enough that some victims can't stand it either, because victims want someone to make an exception. But an exception made for you today will be made for someone with better connections tomorrow.

They care, but not because they understand decentralization better than you.

They care because you don't have their connections, and you can't offer what they can.

With connections and money, you can turn a public road into a private fast lane.
Without them, you wait in line, or get treated as noise.

If you want to protect everyone, you can't only protect the people who can make noise.
Either every address follows the same rules, or admit you're running VIP asset recovery and stop pretending it's about principles.
The wind may enter. The rain may enter. The King may not enter.
What the King is best at isn't talking about morals. It's deciding who deserves to be served.

text:
Asking Grok:
Regarding SecofWar Hegseth's America's Next Great American Base announcement, provide an assessment of placing this base at, or in combination with, Mountain Home AFB in Idaho. Include the following in your assessment:  what other states would have an AFB already established in combination with freeway (I-84) access, ~250 flying days because of weather, nearly unlimited range and growth potential, an already established city, served by a Union Pacific Railroad main freight line, nearby Boise with a major airport. Would Nevada, New Mexico, or Texas offer freeway, rail, commercial air within 50 miles, or desert, forest, mountain training (including survival training) access, possible expansion of the Air Base with an Airlift Wing or Airlift support from McChord AFB

Grok Expert Answer:

Mountain Home AFB (MHAFB) in Idaho is a strong candidate for combination or expansion under the Next Great American Base concept (a new off-grid, hardened joint installation on hundreds of thousands of acres hosting 15,000–25,000 troops, announced 30 September 2026). It already meets most of the listed criteria and offers lower-encroachment growth than many peer sites.

Fit at or with Mountain Home AFB MHAFB (home of the 366th Fighter Wing / “Gunfighters,” primarily F-15E operations plus a Singapore F-15SG detachment) sits on roughly 6,800–9,000 acres in the high desert of Elmore County, about 10–12 miles southwest of the city of Mountain Home and 45–50 miles southeast of Boise via I-84. The real operational advantage is the adjacent Mountain Home Range Complex: Saylor Creek Range (~109,000 acres), Juniper Butte Range (~12,000 acres), and thousands of square miles of Military Operations Areas (MOAs). Combined training airspace is vast (sources cite 9,000+ square nautical miles of special-use airspace or broader figures exceeding 100,000 square miles when including associated areas). Surrounding BLM high-desert land and low population density support large-scale expansion with fewer noise, encroachment, or civilian airspace conflicts than bases near major metros.

I-84 access: Direct. The interstate is the primary corridor through Mountain Home; the base is a short drive off it.

Flying weather: High-desert climate with low precipitation (~11 inches annually), frequent clear skies, and low humidity. One source cites ~224 sunny days; ~250 flying/VFR days is a reasonable estimate consistent with similar arid western bases. Winters are cold and dry; summers hot and arid. Excellent for high-tempo fighter and joint training.

Growth potential: High. Existing ranges plus adjacent undeveloped land allow scaling toward the “hundreds of thousands of acres” target while leveraging current airfield, munitions, and support infrastructure.

Established city: Mountain Home (population ~14,000–15,000) is a classic military-support town built around the base and railroad, with existing housing, schools, and services.

Union Pacific main freight line: Yes. The UP Oregon Short Line / main line runs through Mountain Home. The city acquired a former AFB rail spur and is developing a rail-served industrial park designated as a UP Focus Site. This supports logistics for a large new installation. 

Nearby Boise major airport: Boise Airport (BOI) is ~45–50 miles away with multiple major carriers. This provides commercial air access and family amenities without placing the installation inside a large urban area.

Advantages for the new base: Leverages an existing fighter-wing culture and airfield; diverse nearby training (high desert, Snake River, mountains/forests in the Boise and Sawtooth areas for survival and mountain operations); western CONUS location useful for Pacific-facing or homeland power-projection missions; and a supportive local community. Combining or expanding here would be faster and cheaper than a pure greenfield site.

Limitations: High-desert water constraints (Snake River proximity helps but requires planning); winter cold and wind; relative isolation (mitigated by Boise); and the need for environmental reviews on any large land withdrawal. The existing fighter mission would need integration or relocation planning if the new installation emphasizes different capabilities (e.g., airlift, C2, or autonomous systems).

Comparable existing AFB + interstate + weather + space + city + rail + nearby airport combinationsExact matches are uncommon. Most large western or southwestern fighter/training bases have some but not all elements at once.

Utah (Hill AFB): I-15, near Ogden/Salt Lake City (major airport), rail access, good weather, and some mountain/desert training. More developed surroundings and Wasatch constraints limit “unlimited” expansion compared with Idaho’s high desert.

South Dakota (Ellsworth AFB): I-90, Rapid City airport and city, generally favorable (if more variable) weather. Less rail emphasis and more plains winters; training space exists but not as expansive as MHAFB ranges.

Other inland sites (e.g., certain Texas or New Mexico bases) trade off interstate proximity, commercial-air distance, or training diversity.

Few other locations simultaneously offer an established fighter AFB, a major interstate, a mainline railroad through an existing small city, a nearby mid-sized commercial airport, and truly large-scale high-desert/mountain growth potential with low encroachment.

Nevada, New Mexico, and Texas comparison

Nevada (primarily Nellis AFB / NTTR complex, plus Creech): Strong on several points. I-15 access is excellent; Union Pacific serves Las Vegas; LAS commercial airport is well within 50 miles of Nellis. Desert training is world-class (Nevada Test and Training Range covers thousands of square miles with mountains, valleys, and realistic threat arrays; Red Flag/Green Flag exercises). Mountain and some forest/survival training is available (nearby ranges and Sierra Nevada access). Weather is excellent year-round desert flying. Expansion land exists in the desert north of Las Vegas, but constraints are significant: urban/tourism pressure from Las Vegas, water scarcity, environmental restrictions, and Nellis already functioning as the premier advanced-training hub (less “next new fortress” potential). Airlift-wing addition is feasible but McChord (JBLM, Washington) support would be long-haul; other AMC bases are closer. Overall very capable but more constrained and already heavily utilized than MHAFB.

New Mexico (Holloman AFB near Alamogordo; Cannon AFB near Clovis; Kirtland in Albuquerque): 

Mixed. Holloman sits on US-70 (not a major interstate; I-10/I-25 are 70–90 miles away). Commercial air within 50 miles is limited (small Alamogordo-White Sands Regional); El Paso International is ~90 miles. Rail access is modest. Training is excellent: White Sands Missile Range adjacency provides enormous desert space, plus nearby Sacramento Mountains for mountain/forest/survival work. Expansion potential is high via WSMR. Cannon is more isolated (highways 60/70/84; I-40 farther), with Melrose Range (~70,000 acres) and good high-desert weather, but weaker commercial-air and interstate access. Kirtland has I-25/I-40, a major airport, and rail but is urban with less open-growth land. An airlift wing or McChord support is possible at Holloman/Cannon given existing special-operations and training missions, but logistics distances to McChord remain long. New Mexico offers strong training diversity and space but weaker matches on interstate + 50-mile major commercial air + established small-city rail combo.

Texas (Dyess AFB near Abilene is the closest analog; others include Laughlin, Sheppard): 

Good infrastructure. Dyess has I-20 access, an established city (Abilene), rail, and Abilene Regional Airport (limited commercial service; DFW is farther). Weather is favorable with high VFR percentages (old documentation cited very high flying-day availability). The base already hosts both a bomb wing (B-1) and an airlift wing (317th AW, C-130Js), so adding or expanding airlift is straightforward. West Texas offers space for growth and some ranges; mountain/forest/survival training is more limited (plains/mesquite terrain) than Idaho or New Mexico mountains. Expansion is feasible in rural areas. McChord support is possible but not geographically convenient. Texas sites generally score well on logistics and existing airlift but less uniquely on combined desert + mountain/forest training variety and “unlimited” low-encroachment desert ranges compared with MHAFB.

Bottom line: Combining or expanding at Mountain Home AFB aligns unusually well with the stated criteria—existing AFB infrastructure + I-84 + strong flying weather + massive range/growth potential + small established city + UP mainline + Boise commercial air—while adding nearby mountain, river, and forest training options. Nevada’s Nellis complex is operationally elite but more constrained. New Mexico and Texas offer viable alternatives with different trade-offs (training scale vs. interstate/commercial-air proximity vs. existing airlift). A merit-based competition would weigh red-tape reduction, land packages, and community support; Idaho’s low-density high desert and existing ranges give it a practical edge for rapid, large-scale development of a self-sustaining “fortress” installation.

text:
Women and Madness by @phyllischesler

To my surprise, Google sent me this notice. I otherwise would not have known any of this. I guess it’s a very good thing, to be so privileged so as to have written a book that has traveled around the world and through time to reach so many readers. See the review below, in Romania Journal.

It’s been 54 years since I first published it. I might be the only one alive now who stands able and willing to criticize its shortcomings, blind spots, limitations. I might also want to expand it quite a bit. I did so, only once, when I wrote a new introduction to it in 2005. But I did not go far enough. ‘Tis true, many of the themes in Women and Madness I developed further in my other nineteen books.

Once, the woman who read this work for an audiobook, perhaps a decade ago, perhaps a bit less, called me and said: “How relevant, how timely your book remains.”

I responded: “Oh, that is so depressing to hear.”

She was, of course, amazed, confused, but then I explained: “I had hoped that women would have come a bit further by now...”

Then there is this. I know too much about the history of the Jews in Romania, in Lithuania, and under the rule of the Turkish Ottoman Empire to be entirely happy about sharing a work by a Jewish author, a Jewish woman. Just read the memoir written by Ruth Kluger, with the assistance of her friend Peggy Mann, to understand what happened to Romanian Jews in the 1930s and very early 1940s.

For years, I refused to allow this book to appear in Spain in honor of the Abraham Lincoln Brigade and because Franco ruled the country. But then, I caught hold of myself and regretted this choice--Woman and Madness is now in Spanish. (Jews did not have an easy time of it in Spain either; we still don’t.)

Anyway, my work has also appeared in Japan, China, and South Korea--and when that happened, I felt that I’d crossed a sound barrier of sorts. This is the only book of mine that has been translated into Hebrew. This is a great puzzlement indeed.

I consider all this humbly, but also as truly great birthday presents. I turn 86 tomorrow on October 1st. Always, my birthday is always close to the Jewish New Year, to God’s creation of the world. We are all “b’zalmo” and contain holy sparks, divine light--you, me, all humanity.

Women and Madness: The Groundbreaking Book Changing Psychiatry

“Women and Madness”, the Pioneering Book That Changed the Way We Talk About Women and Mental Health.

Sep 29, 2026

Romania Journal

“Why can a woman be considered mentally ill when asserting her sexual, economic, or intellectual autonomy?”, “Why are women pathologized, instead of receiving support, when they react naturally to abuse and stress, including the long-term stress associated with second-class citizenship status?“. These are two of the essential questions to which Dr. Phyllis Chesler, one of the iconic figures of feminism, offers answers in the book Women and Madness.

Published for the first time in Romanian by Editura Trei, in the “Psihologia pentru toți” (Psychology for All) collection, the volume—which has sold over 3 million copies worldwide over time—analyzes how women have been understood, diagnosed, and treated within the medical and psychological system.

Described as “intense, incisive, remarkable” and bringing “a pioneering contribution to transforming psychiatric thought and practice through a feminist lens,” according to The New York Times Book Review, Women and Madness was the first work to address openly and candidly the relationship between women’s status and the social norms that converted difference and psychological distress into punitive labels. 

Starting from this premise, Dr. Phyllis Chesler questions the very definition of madness and how this label was applied as a diagnosis for the purposes of invalidation and erasure. Throughout the chapters, she exposes the distorted lens through which women were viewed and, often, removed from communities or their own families through psychiatric diagnoses, institutionalized, and abused in asylums. Interweaving accounts from 60 women who lived through such experiences with an analysis of women’s roles in real life, literature, and mythology, Chesler highlights this dangerous double standard by which women are judged psychologically and psychiatrically.

In this landmark volume—not only for psychology, but also for history and the universal understanding of women’s status—Phyllis Chesler traces, drawing on her professional and life experience across many countries and diverse societies, how these standards vary according to gender, race, social status, or sexual orientation, offering a broad perspective on women’s experiences in different cultural contexts.

First published in 1972, Women and Madness was received extraordinarily well by female readers. Garnering hundreds of positive reviews, it was translated into numerous languages, including Japanese and Hebrew. As the author shares in the book’s introduction, she received over 10,000 letters from readers, which she kept and which confirmed her theories.

 In contrast, within academia and among professionals in the field, her analysis regarding the use of diagnostic labels to stigmatize women, alongside her explanation of why more women than men—regardless of behavior—became psychiatric patients, were ignored, dismissed as sensationalist, or harshly criticized. 

Her statistics and theories were declared “wrong,” and Chesler was accused of exaggerating regarding the institutions of marriage and psychiatry, as well as “over-romanticizing” archetypes, particularly those of goddesses and Amazons. “Like many feminists before me, I became a ‘circus dog’ on the feminist academic and professional circuit. 

Fortunately, I was on the verge of obtaining a tenured position at a university; and also fortunately, neither my father, nor my brother, nor my husband wanted to lock me in a psychiatric hospital because my ideas offended them,” she notes, referencing the accounts detailed in the book and the experiences lived by many women.

Revised and updated in 2005, the book also addresses issues that grew in significance in the decades following its initial release: eating disorders, pressure from beauty standards, depression, anxiety, addictions, sexuality, and postpartum depression. The book’s new introduction analyzes the trauma associated with psychiatric labeling and proposes the perspective of a psychology of liberation.

More than five decades after its initial publication, Women and Madness retains its power and relevance through an incisive voice that continues to spark debates about authority, power, and women’s place in society.

Phyllis Chesler is Professor Emerita of Psychology and Women’s Studies at the City University of New York. A bestselling author, iconic feminist figure, psychotherapist, and expert witness, Dr. Chesler has published thousands of articles and, in recent years, numerous studies on the violence behind honor killings.

 Besides Women and Madness, she has authored several landmark books, including Mothers on Trial: The Battle for Children and Custody and Woman’s Inhumanity to Woman.

Throughout her career, she has led campaigns and lectured across Europe, the Middle East, and the Far East.

She is the co-founder of the Association for Women in Psychology (founded in 1969), the National Women’s Health Network (founded in 1974), and the International Committee for the Jerusalem-based Women of the Wall (founded in 1989).

She has appeared on shows such as The Today Show and The O’Reilly Factor. With over 4 million online references related to her work, Dr. Chesler has been featured in numerous encyclopedias, including Feminists Who Have Changed America, Jewish Women in America, and the latest edition of Encyclopaedia 

Subscribe to Phyllis’s Newsletter.  @Phyllischesler

• Assistance is not replacement.

• Guidance is not substitution.

• Love does not mean that somebody else lives your incarnation for you.

• Before the civilization, who are you?

• Before you ever called yourself a Starseed, what was present?

• There is consciousness.

• Some of you have spent many incarnational experiences in forms that were not Earth human.

• Some of you feel Earth is familiar, and some of you have never entirely felt that way.

• But none of this is offered so that you can feel superior to the people around you.

• It is offered to loosen the belief that this current human expression is the total boundary of your existence.

• You are not a human trying to obtain a soul.

• You are soul presently expressing through a human biological instrument.

A college rape case has ignited the country. Let's talk about what we're actually talking about here

https://t.co/imUbY0C3og

"The alleged details of this case are wrenching and sickening: A young woman went to a fraternity party to meet a guy she thought was her friend. They danced and drank, and, according to her statement to police, the first man asked Jane Doe if she would have a threesome with him and another friend; she said she agreed largely because she wanted to please the first guy. But then other guys entered the room; Jane Doe reports hiding under the covers and pushing various men’s hands away as they grabbed at her. She says the men offered her ketamine, and she took it, and as the night progressed she became extremely intoxicated, and other men had sex with her. Not mentioned in the police report but highlighted in the lawsuit is that some of the men were on Snapchat, sending messages about there being “free pussy” available and inviting other men to come over and join in.

The case of the “Cornell Seven,” the seven former fraternity members accused of drugging and gang-raping a 20-year-old woman, is a disturbing one. The alleged assault occurred in 2024, but criminal charges were not brought; now, the woman is suing her alleged assailants, as well as their fraternity, her former sorority, Cornell University, and the bar that served her alcohol that night. The men deny any wrongdoing; the district attorney says he had good reasons for not bringing a criminal case; and the university says it responded appropriately at the time. Much of the public seems to disagree, and there have been growing calls for criminal sanctions. As of this week, the Tompkins County district attorney has reopened the criminal case.

The alleged details of this case are wrenching and sickening: A young woman went to a fraternity party to meet a guy she thought was her friend. They danced and drank, and, according to her statement to police, the first man asked Jane Doe if she would have a threesome with him and another friend; she said she agreed largely because she wanted to please the first guy. But then other guys entered the room; Jane Doe reports hiding under the covers and pushing various men’s hands away as they grabbed at her. She says the men offered her ketamine, and she took it, and as the night progressed she became extremely intoxicated, and other men had sex with her. Not mentioned in the police report but highlighted in the lawsuit is that some of the men were on Snapchat, sending messages about there being “free pussy” available and inviting other men to come over and join in.

It’s that last fact—the Snapchat messages—that has most infuriated much of the public. And it should. It should be at the center of the conversation about sexual violence, consent, and male entitlement to women’s bodies. And as much as the public’s understanding of sexual violence has grown more sophisticated in the wake of various waves of the feminist movement and the gains made by #MeToo, the truth is that we are still abysmal when it comes to understanding, let alone publicly discussing, the ways in which sex, power, and male violence intersect.

The Cornell case is a complex one, which makes it all the more difficult to traverse—to go beyond the legalese and actually talk about what we’re talking about. The demands for criminal prosecution have grown so loud that, in an unusual move, the district attorney published a letter explaining why he didn’t bring those charges in the first place. New York’s rape law is narrow: Sex with a person who is extremely intoxicated but conscious doesn’t count as rape if the alleged victim voluntarily drank or took drugs (as opposed to being secretly drugged or forced to drink). According to the DA, “Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.” He then published part of the statement signed by Jane Doe.

Whether that statement truly captures an interaction that was “voluntary, conscious, and consensual” seems less clear to me than it does to prosecutors. One also wonders why Jane Doe brought herself to the police station in the first place if all she had to report was voluntary, conscious, and consensual group sex—most people don’t have great fun consensual sex and then report it to the cops...

the particulars of the law might explain why the DA didn’t bring charges two years ago. But it doesn’t absolve the men or the institutions (Cornell, the DA’s office) involved. It doesn’t answer the larger social question that animates so many of these cases: How should we treat other human beings? Why do we shrug when men so often treat women so horribly? Why do we still presume that men simply are sexually predatory, extractive, and coercive, and that it’s on women to be the ever-vigilant guardians of sexual morality? And what should the social consequences be for behavior that is appalling, sadistic, and damaging, even if (especially if) it doesn’t meet the current definition of a crime?

In this case, Jane Doe filed a lawsuit seeking damages, not criminal penalties or jail time (only a prosecutor can seek those). She is saying: These men did something egregiously wrong, and even if prosecutors didn’t believe it met the requirements for criminal prosecution under New York law, it was still wrong, and they should still pay a price. She’s also saying that Cornell didn’t respond appropriately. The school did shut down the fraternity and expelled two of the men, but the rest were allowed to stay with various disciplinary procedures; some reportedly saw their penalties decreased after they wrote essays. Her life has stalled out; theirs have ticked on."

text:
🇺🇸 Nakashima vs. Humbert 🇫🇷

Brandon Nakashima arrives in Tokyo playing some of the best tennis of his career, posting a 22–10 record on hard courts this season and coming off a strong showing at the Laver Cup, where he beat Jakub Menšík 6–1, 3–6, 10–7. The American reached the quarterfinals here last year, and his clean, compact baseline game and excellent backhand return make him especially effective at neutralizing big servers and dictating rallies on medium-paced hard courts.

Ugo Humbert has historically had Nakashima's number, holding a clear edge in their head-to-head, including a 6–3, 6–2 win on this court two years ago during his run to the Tokyo final. However, the Frenchman enters this match in a very different situation. He withdrew from the U.S. Open with a recurring back injury, has not played a match since losing in Cincinnati in mid-August, and is just 8–10 on hard courts this season. For a left-hander whose game relies on first-strike serving and aggressive, flat ball-striking, any lingering back issue is a major concern.

text:
Did Texas AG Paxton let Adam Hoffman get away with child sex abuse ?
Paxton’s AG office approved a plea that reduced Adam Hoffman’s case from a first-degree felony (continuous sexual abuse of a child, 25 years to life) to two misdemeanors after a hung jury; Hoffman served 29 days and avoided Texas sex-offender registration.
https://t.co/vvy5SMtT18
Hoffman, a former Waco attorney, was arrested in 2022 and accused of repeatedly abusing his son’s friend over roughly three years beginning when the boy was about 7–8. McLennan County DA Josh Tetens recused because Hoffman had previously consulted him, so Paxton’s office handled the prosecution. The June 2025 trial ended in a hung jury (7-5 for conviction). Prosecutors later said the victim would not testify again and that they lacked a path to a felony conviction without that testimony.
https://t.co/mJrlYEfeH3
In April 2026 they offered a deal: guilty pleas to Class A misdemeanors (indecent assault and display of harmful material to a minor). The plea language did not specify the victim’s age, which is why Hoffman was not required to register as a sex offender in Texas. The initial proposed jail time was time served plus one day. The judge rejected that as too light, first raising it to 30 days plus a five-year license surrender, then to 60 days after public outcry. Hoffman was released after 29 days under the county’s good-time policy. He later moved to Nebraska, where he is required to register. A lifetime no-contact order with the victim was also part of the final deal.
https://t.co/4ZWJvQAmEy
Paxton has defended the outcome as protecting the child from a second trial rather than “letting him get away.” Critics—including James Talarico, John Cornyn during the GOP primary, and the victim’s mother—call it a sweetheart deal for a well-connected defendant (Hoffman’s lawyer had also represented Nate Paul, a Paxton associate). Talarico has demanded release of internal AG files on the case. The office’s stated rationale is documented in a letter prosecutors sent to a state lawmaker who questioned the deal.
https://t.co/rR3iQLAFhJ
Whether this constitutes “letting him get away” is a matter of judgment: the felony charge was dropped, the sentence was far shorter than the original exposure, and Texas registration was avoided, all after the AG’s office took the case. The alternative they cited was no conviction at all if the victim refused to testify a second time.

The three cases

1.  La Vernia High School (2017 arrests)
Texas Rangers and the AG’s office took over a Wilson County hazing investigation involving varsity athletes accused of sodomizing younger teammates with objects (flashlight, Gatorade bottle, CO2 tank, etc.). At least 13 students were charged, some as adults, with sexual assault or related offenses, including assault of a minor. The AG’s office offered plea deals to multiple defendants. Several pleaded to lesser charges such as unlawful restraint or hazing, received deferred adjudication or probation, served no jail time, and were eligible for record expungement. Nine accepted such deals. This was reported contemporaneously in 2019 by local outlets.

by Artist Michael Rucker

Description
Beauseant at Montgisard 1177
Era: High Middle Ages Kingdom of Jerusalem, 25 November 1177

Gallery description
This painting places a Templar knight at the heart of one of the most improbable victories of the Crusades. On 25 November 1177, sixteen-year-old King Baldwin IV of Jerusalem already marked by leprosy rode out with a few hundred knights to stop Saladins Ayyubid army from reaching the Holy City. With him came Grand Master Eudes de Saint-Amand and roughly eighty Knights Templar from Gaza. 

Contemporary estimates give the Christians perhaps 375450 knights and several thousand infantry against a far larger Muslim host that had been allowed to scatter while raiding. Saladin, confident the leper king would stay behind walls, was caught crossing broken ground near Montgisard (Tell Gezer / Mons Gisardi), between Ramla and Yibna. Baldwin knelt before a fragment of the True Cross, then ordered the charge. The Templars formed the spearhead. Their war banner, the Beauseant black above white, black to enemies, white to friends was the signal that no brother might quit the field while it still flew. 

The shock of heavy cavalry smashed the unready Ayyubid line. Saladin himself barely escaped; most of his army did not.The scene you see is not a portrait of one named man but an emblem of that hour: white mantle and red cross pattee of the Temple, kite shield, the Beauseant replacing later anachronisms, stone churches of the Latin East rising behind the dust. It is offered so visitors may remember that history is not only catastrophe. Sometimes a small, disciplined force, a young king who would not hide, and a banner that meant we do not leave changed the map for a season.

Baldwins victory bought the Kingdom of Jerusalem nearly a decade. Saladin would return; Hattin and the fall of Jerusalem still lay ahead. Yet Montgisard remains the day the Temples black-and-white standard flew over a field that should have been lost.Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam.

< Born 1755, a log cabin on the Virginia frontier
< No formal schooling until you're 14
< Your father is friends with George Washington. This will matter.

< You leave the war hating one thing above all: state weakness.
< Back in Virginia, you teach yourself law in six weeks of lectures.
< Pass the bar. Start a practice. Marry Polly Ambler.
< You argue cases in a rumpled coat, mud on your boots.
< Other lawyers dress like English lords. You dress like you just walked in from a farm.
< Juries love it.
< Virginia sends you to the state ratifying convention. You argue for the Constitution.
< Patrick Henry argues against. He's the most famous orator in America.
< You win anyway. Virginia ratifies by 10 votes.
< President Adams offers you Secretary of State. You take it.
< Then Adams loses the 1800 election to Jefferson. Your cousin. Your enemy.
< Adams has one card left to play. The Chief Justice seat is empty.
< He nominates you. The Senate confirms in one day.
< Jefferson is inaugurated two weeks later. Too late.
< You will serve 34 years. The longest tenure of any Chief Justice in history.
< The Court you inherit has no power. It meets in a basement.
< Marbury v. Madison, 1803. A minor case about a minor appointment.
< You rule against Marbury. Jefferson's team celebrates.

< Judicial review. You invented it. Nobody voted for it.
< McCulloch v. Maryland. You rule Congress can create a national bank.

< You take it as a compliment.
< Polly dies in 1831. You wear a locket of her hair until your own death.
< 1835. You are 79. You fall, injure your spine, and never recover.

The Constitution doesn't mention judicial review once.

Washington State 

PUBLIC GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEE UNIONS STATE LEGISLATURE 

Legislative staff in Washington state Senate reject new contract

Employees for Democratic senators wanted stronger job security provisions. Legislative assistants for Republican lawmakers have ratified their agreements.

Sept. 30, 2026

The union representing staff of Democratic state senators in Washington has overwhelmingly rejected a new two-year contract, citing its lack of adequate protections for workers facing termination.

Legislative assistants, policy analysts and communications specialists for the Senate Democratic Caucus on Monday voted down the final offer from negotiators for the Senate Administration. The employees are represented by the Washington Public Employees Association.

The rejected deal contained no pay hike, only a provision to renew talks on wages next August, mirroring language in collective bargaining agreements with most other public sector unions amid state budget struggles.

But the lack of a raise wasn’t the sticking point for those who work for the Senate’s majority party.

Their concern centered on job security. Legislative staff are at-will employees, meaning they can be fired at any time. The union sought language to ensure there is a just cause for a dismissal. Negotiators for the administration wouldn’t budge on various proposals employees put forth, union officials said.

“Our fight is not with the electeds, it is with the administration,” stressed Sam Hines-Tinsley, legislative specialist for the union. “Members of our bargaining team made it clear that they were looking for fundamental change and for fair, reasonable and predictable treatment when it comes to discipline.”

Jeremy Knapp, a Senate legislative assistant, said in a statement that his colleagues know “we can be let go for no reason, and while we know we may not get economic security, we need more job security. All we’re asking for is the same due process that almost every represented public sector worker in Washington has.”

Officials from the Senate Administration did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

State law sets an Oct. 1 deadline for public worker unions to submit ratified agreements to the Office of Financial Management to be considered for funding in the next two-year budget.

For Senate employees, their decision Monday means that when the current contract expires next July, most of its provisions will be extended until a new collective bargaining agreement is ratified.

Their counterparts working for the House Democratic Caucus could be in a similar situation within hours as they were still locked in contract talks Wednesday afternoon.

In contrast, the legislative assistants in the House and Senate Republican caucuses have approved their respective two-year agreements.

“Under the circumstances, given the position the state is in, we were OK with what was presented,” said Rob Barnes, president of the Legislative Professionals Association that represents the aides to Republican lawmakers in each chamber.

Last Friday, members of the Washington Federation of State Employees, the largest union of state government workers, ratified their two-year contract after months of tense talks and informational picketing. 

Federation units representing workers in community colleges, universities and administrative law judges also approved their contracts.

Earlier this week, the Washington Public Employees Association reported its units representing around 5,300 general government and community college employees had narrowly voted to approve new collective bargaining agreements. These cover workers at 14 community colleges and nine state agencies, including the Department of Natural Resources, Department of Revenue, the Liquor and Cannabis Board and Department of Agriculture.
